speechtext:
Mr. Drew asks for leave under standing order 26 to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of public importance. He has indicated that the matter in question is the need for a definite government policy regarding the shipments from Canada to foreign countries of arms, military equipment and ammunition and the effective supervision thereof.
As the house knows, according to standing order 26, it rests with the Speaker to decide, not only whether the motion for leave is in order, but also whether in his opinion, that is, in the Speaker's opinion, he thinks that it is of urgent public importance. Under our practice, a matter of urgent public importance is understood to be one with regard to which there is urgency of debate.
I do not know to what extent I should preserve the line of reasoning that I and many of my predecessors have followed, namely, that whenever there is a debate like the one currently going on, which gives the opportunity to hon. members to discuss a wide range of subjects, motions such as this one have not been allowed. I am inclined today to follow the precedents that have been established. Today is the seventh appointed day of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. There are still three more days.
We all know that the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn), who adjourned the debate last night, will shortly obtain the
floor and, on the basis of our memory of what has happened in previous sessions, is likely to move another subamendment which will give hon. members the right to speak for 40 minutes each. Therefore they can debate at great length the matter proposed for this day in the motion now before me. In view of that I would submit that all those who wish to put forward points with regard to this matter can take advantage of the debate which is going to follow shortly on the amendment to the amendment about to be moved by the hon. member for New Westminster. In these circumstances I do not think I would be justified in accepting the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I announced in this house on June 3 last that the federal government was prepared to pay a subsidy of $25,000 per mile for not more than 50 miles of a northward extension of the Pacific Great Eastern from Prince George. I stated that the government did not believe a through line to the Peace river valley was economically justified at that time. 1 pointed out, in support of that contention, that the Peace river area already has rail access through the Northern Alberta railways and that, although this railway taps the greater part of the area, it does not obtain a sufficient volume of traffic to result in profitable operations.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, January 19, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Shipley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset compliment you on the capable way in which you conduct the office of Speaker of the house. I should also like to compliment the members of the 

cabinet who show such dexterity and capability in side-stepping the issues at hand. If I may say so, I am almost inclined to say that they show as much dexterity and skill as did the New Westminster soccer club in winning the dominion championship last year. I should like at this time to ease the mind of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) by announcing that it is my intention to submit an amendment which will give him the opportunity to discuss the question he wanted to discuss, and after the present debate is finished possibly he could continue its discussion by means of such a motion as he has in mind.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley), in the course of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne, said in effect that she could not understand why so much valuable time should be taken up by member after member repeating what had been said in other words by many other members. I hope she will forgive me therefore if I add my congratulations to the others with which she has been showered because through her I wish to congratulate the women of Canada and the constituents whom she has the honour to represent. I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Laflamme) on the capable way in which he conducted himself, and also the newly elected members of the house who I am sure will represent their constituencies ably and well.
During the course of the past two years when I have been in the house it has been my privilege to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) the need for a secondary airport to supplement the Vancouver international airport. It was with great pleasure therefore that I read the press release on January 12 that he had seen fit to accept the advice of some of his colleagues and possibly accept the thought I had in mind, that the White Rock airport would be a good secondary airport. The choice is well taken because the White Rock airport will lend itself to expansion. It is off the main air routes and is fog free. It is away from any military air base so that there probably will not be any danger of a tragedy similar to the one that occurred at Moose Jaw last year. It is also a short distance from Vancouver.
I wish to express gratitude to the minister and to anyone else who may have had anything whatsoever to do with the final decision that White Rock should be the secondary airport. I was pleased to see that the minister indicated in his news release that there was need for examination into the possibility of finding another site suitable for small craft.
I trust such a site will be found before all the possible sites are used for other purposes.

During the past few days the discussion in this debate has been concerned principally with the question of grain surpluses. Other surpluses were also mentioned. The question of cheese was raised by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) referred to the question of dairy products.
The hon. member for Wellington-Huron (Mr. Howe) mentioned butter. Yesterday the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) dealt with potatoes. One might ask what brings about this cry. The real reason behind it, Mr. Speaker, is that the farmers have a right to expect a fair share of the national income. As pertinent to that matter, I have here a compilation of some figures respecting percentages of total national income received by farmers by years. It is not my intention to read all these figures but I should like you to note that during the years 1915, 1916, 1917, 1918 and 1919, when the farmers represented about 30 per cent of the population of Canada, their share of the national income was 30 per cent. From 1926 to 1928 the number of farmers was less than that-it would be from 25 per cent to 30 per cent-and their share of the income dropped to the point where it was from 17 per cent to 14-6 per cent. During the depression years from 1929 to 1939 the share of the national income that the farmers received was reduced tremendously, to an all time low of a 4-1 per cent in 1933 while the farm population represented a little better than 20 per cent of Canada's over-all population. During this past year the share of the national income received by the farmers was 6-7 per cent. Yet they represent 20 per cent of Canada's population today. In effect that situation would indicate that the share of the national income received by the farmers compares approximately with what they received in 1934, which was a grave depression year.
During the war years, because of price stabilization and price control as set down by the government, the share of the national income received by the farmers rose to approximately 11 per cent. As was explained yesterday by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), the reason for that situation was that the farmer was promised a better deal after the war in order to compensate for the low price he was accepting for his commodities. Since the war, of course, we have had a continual decline in farm income with the result that I mentioned earlier, namely that today the farmers are in effect receiving about the same percentage of the national income as they were receiving during the depression year of 1934.
The Address-Mr. Hahn
As far as my riding is concerned the problem is this. While there happens to be a grain terminal in my riding, it is not my desire to talk about grain at this time although I must say I could do so. The problem in my particular riding in this instance is that of the potato grower. He is not getting his fair share of the national income. One might say: Is this a national problem? It is definitely a national problem because, on reading the report made by a committee set up to study the question of potatoes last year, I discover that the potato industry is of major importance in every province in Canada except the province of Newfoundland. Therefore these people whose livelihood is so greatly affected should be given the consideration to which they are entitled. This particular committee, which was set up last year at the behest of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), was to hear representations but was not to make recommendations. The hearings were set for June of last year in the city of Ottawa and representations were made by the various potato growing groups across the nation. I would draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, pages 60 and 61 of their report. Eleven conclusions are arrived at. All of them are reasonable and sound. However, I would say that two of the conclusions definitely carry with them an inference or a recommendation which possibly affected the government's decision not to take any action on the tariff question last year. I would draw to your attention particularly conclusion No. 8 on page 61, which is as follows:
Geared by force of geography to reliance upon export markets-whether elsewhere in Canada or abroad-the industry in Prince Edward Island is very greatly dependent for its continuance upon the demand at home and abroad for its certified seed potatoes.
That statement is perfectly correct but we have here an inference in the conclusion:
Loss of its seed-potato quota in the United States would be but short of disastrous for the island and only somewhat less so for New Brunswick.
Mr. Speaker, the inference is that by the setting up of a tariff the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island would lose their seed potato market. In reply to that contention I would say that the potato growers of New Brunswick and of Prince Edward Island have a high quality seed as well as a disease-free seed. That is the actual reason for the American people buying seed potatoes from them. They buy them because they need them, not because they particularly want to buy seed potatoes from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.

The Address-Mr. Hahn
The other inference is included in conclusion No. 10 of the report which is as follows:
While no rigid generalization can be made, because of occasional and quite abnormal variations from the rule, such imports of table potatoes from the United States as do occur, appear to be attracted to this market by higher domestic prices which in turn frequently reflect a short crop in Canada.
That part of the statement is true. However, here is the inference:
So called "new potatoes"-imported into this country during the spring and early summer months-command a premium because they are new; and probably would enter whether or not they faced a customs duty at the border.
The suggestion then is that there would be no value in putting a tariff duty in effect because these new potatoes would come in no matter what the price might be, and that there would be no stopping them. Those inferences should not be included in the report and the government should not have taken them into consideration. However, they apparently must have done so, the facts being what they are in the potato industry today. There is need for some action by the government in respect of protecting the potato grower.
The developments since the hearings were held in Ottawa in June-and there were several-are as follows. The first was definite action taken by United States authorities in respect of the size of potatoes that would be allowed to come into their country and which affected our market. I wish to thank the government for taking action on this particular question and bringing cur regulations in line with those of the United States.
There is, however, another question which is more important and which affects the industry more greatly. I refer to the announcement made by secretary of agriculture Benson of the United States. On August 26 he announced that the United States department of agriculture extends financial assistance to those United States producer states which sign an agreement to show an approved plan which will eliminate, by various means, 20 per cent or more of marketable grade 2 or better potatoes. This program was to begin on September 26, 1955.
If the hon. gentlemen opposite who are from British Columbia wish to take part in this discussion, they may do so later.

speechtext: We never said a word.

speechtext: I was not paying attention. I do not know what you are talking about.

speechtext:
Diversion of grade 2 or better to starch, feed or flour was called for by the regulation.

Now, the fact of the matter in this instance is that the United States authorities were going to pay $10 a ton for the period from September 26 to December 31 last year; $8 until March 31 and $6 until June 30, 1956. In effect, this would act as a subsidy to those U.S. growers who were getting less than the normal price for their potatoes. Now, the conclusion that I must draw from this is that the assistance that was being given to the United States potato grower on potatoes diverted to these other industries was nothing more or less than a subsidy. In the retail trade this procedure is covered by the phrase, what I lose on the coffee I make up on the beans. So far as the United States grower was concerned, what he was losing on his table potato crop he was going to gain on the crop that was being diverted.
The Department of National Revenue says that this is not dumping. In reply to this particular question there is a letter dated September 20 from Mr. D. Sim, deputy minister of national revenue, at Ottawa, in which he says:
Section 6 (A). as recently enacted by parliament, empowers the governor in council to impose an additional duty equal to the amount ot subsidy on the goods, but provides that where the imported goods are also subject to special or dumping duty under section 6 (say by reason ot an export subsidy) -
That is the important phrase.
-the amount ot the additional duty under section 6 (A) shall be reduced by the amount of the special or dumping duty under section 6.
The argument is that the potatoes that are being sent into Canada, while they are being exported, are not subject to this assistance because they do not come under the diversion plan. Technically, that is quite correct, but if you give a farmer $10 in another way as a bonus or anything else, that is going to make it possible for him to eventually give his potatoes away. It should be called dumping for the same reason.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in my own riding of New Westminster and the lower Fraser valley this has had a marked effect upon the potato growing industry. Last year, according to figures I have here, between June 1 and June 15, a time at which United States potatoes were being imported, the British Columbia potato growers association could only sell 197 tons of their own potatoes while United States imports amounted to 3,382 tons. From June 18 to July 2, a period when the duty was being imposed, the United States exported 1,244 tons which made a grand total of 4,626 tons of potatoes that were imported from the United States. During that time the B.C. grower could only sell 197 tons. In July the B.C. grower sold 3,482 tons and at the same time the United States exported to

us some 1,327 tons. I might say that by this time the United States grower had skimmed the cream off the crop, as any person from British Columbia will recognize when they sold us 4,626 tons to July, for that is when the new potatoes come on the market and the United States growers were able to get high prices for them.
Then later, in August, the British Columbia grower was only able to sell 3,027 tons while the United States growers sold 2,805 tons. This made a total for the three months period for the B.C. grower of 6,787 tons, while the United States grower sold 8,788 tons in the same period. There is only six weeks' protection period for the potato grower in Canada. The figures were not available for the rest of the year, but the British Columbia coast marketing vegetable board had this to say in a release in October. They put out a regular bulletin, I should say, Mr. Speaker, from which this extract is taken in October, 1955:
Imports of potatoes from the United States into the Vancouver market for the four-week period September 5 through 30th amounted to 1,455 tons. White varieties have moved fairly well up to the present date. However, it was found necessary by your board to drop the price on netted Gem potatoes by $6 per ton to be competitive with shipments being received from across the border. The Yakima market declined from $43 per ton on September 16 to $32 per ton on October 1.
Now, looking at the figure very quickly, one would say the United States market declined by $11 per ton, but the United States grower was getting a $10 subsidy for every ton of potatoes he was diverting at that time into another field. His market, therefore, declined by only $1 per ton, but the B.C. grower at that time had his market drop by $6 per ton in order to be competitive. The additional loss suffered by the United States grower would be made up by diverting 20 per cent of his other potatoes into the United States feed and flour business. This is one of my reasons for saying that this diversion scheme the United States has invoked at this time is, in effect, a subsidy. It is one of the arguments into which I would ask the minister to look very closely.
The December bulletin issued by this same organization, the British Columbia coast vegetable marketing board, had this to say:
Closer to the border, the growers directly across the line have this past week approached the trade in Vancouver .	.	. offering to sell their
Ho. 1 Gem potatoes at $2 below the prevailing Vancouver board price. Your board had declined to reduce the price of No. 1 Gems as it felt that these shippers would only again cut below us.
You can only go so far in reducing the price of your potatoes or any other commodity. You can hope that something will happen that will protect your market, and 67509-23
The Address-Mr. Hahn possibly you will be free to sell at a later time. Fortunately, that did happen for the B.C. potato grower in November. Heavy frosts in the Pacific northwest, which unfortunately wiped out almost every nurseryman and every small fruit grower, had a good effect so far as the B.C. potato grower was concerned. As a result of the frost it was not possible for the United States potatoes to come into the B.C. market, and the B.C. grower was able to sell his own potatoes in the lower mainland area of British Columbia.
Imports into Canada for the first seven months of 1955, as compared with 1954, are as follows. In 1954 imports amounted to 1,057,947 cwt., and in 1955 they amounted to 1,987,089 cwt.

speechtext: What about export?

speechtext:
I have not the figure for export, I am sorry. However, our exports are quite negligible because they consist of seed potatoes which would go to the United States in any event because they are short of quality seed. The authority for that statement will be found in this tariff board hearing. The fact is that in 1954 we imported only about one million cwt. of potatoes, and in 1955 we imported very nearly two million cwt. In other words, last year the American potato grower was able to sell twice as many potatoes in our country as he had done theretofore. Naturally, that has its effect on the Canadian potato market. Not only is the subsidy having an effect on the price and the sales we make, but this matter of importing potatoes in such heavy quantities is bound to affect the potato grower in Canada.
There was an editorial in the British Columbian of January 17, 1956-I may say that the British Columbian is a daily newspaper within the area I represent-which had this to say:
The British Columbia coast vegetable marketing board and growers in British Columbia have attempted to bring the intolerable situation to the attention of the federal authorities for several years.
This is the matter of tariffs on potatoes. The article goes on to say:
Coast producers do not think the starch subsidy is the answer,-
That is the starch subsidy that the Minister of Agriculture pointed out yesterday we were putting into effect. I continue:
-and remark that the hope such a subsidy "will help maintain prices across Canada is merely wishful thinking on the part of the federal department of agriculture inasmuch as Canadian prices are governed by the heavy imports from the United States whose product often enters Canada at below actual cost of production of either United States or Canadian growers."

The Address-Mr. Hahn
The grower in the United States has a tremendous market for his goods, and the small amount that he sends to Canada does not affect his market at all; it does not affect his wealth. He is just getting rid of a small surplus. On the other hand, the Canadian producer finds that the potatoes that come in from the United States affect his price and his market a great deal.
The speeches that were made in the past few days with respect to surpluses were actually unwarranted, although I will say they were necessary. I say they were unwarranted for the reason that if the government were to examine into the possibility of the two-price system that was proposed by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), I am satisfied that most of the economic ills in the agricultural and primary producing fields would be adequately looked after.
As I indicated earlier, it is my intention to move an amendment to the amendment. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Yuill):
That the amendment be amended by inserting after the words "by reason of", the following:
1.	Their failure to adopt and implement agricultural and marketing policies designed effectively to keep farm cash income in Canada at a just and economic level.
2.	Their utter neglect of any responsibility with regard to assisting the provinces to maintain a satisfactorily broad tax base through adequate development of their resources, and-
The amendment as amended would then read thus:
We respectfully represent that Your Excellency's advisers, by reason of
1.	Their failure to adopt and implement agricultural and marketing policies designed effectively to keep farm cash income in Canada at a just and economic level.
2.	Their utter neglect of any responsibility with regard to assisting the provinces to maintain a satisfactorily broad tax base through adequate development of their resources, and their indifference, inertia, and lack of leadership in the face of serious national problems and their disregard of the rights of parliament, are not entitled to the confidence of this house.

speechtext: That is a good one. The hon. member has everything in it but baling wire.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Give me time, and I will have it in there, too. There are ranchers in the country who could tell you something about the price of baling wire, and perhaps it should be included.
I would agree with the hon. member for Jasper-Edson who the day before yesterday raised the question of the sale of butter. His proposal and his method of disposing of it through those who are in need of social security, such as the aged, the blind, the disabled, the war veterans, and others, are

worthy of consideration. I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that if we are to give something to the people behind the iron curtain we should not give away our butter. Let us give away margarine and let us keep the butter for the people in Canada. Let us sell the butter to the people of Canada at the price at which we sell margarine. I am satisfied that the people of Canada would enjoy butter, and some of them would get in the position where they would begin to use it again.
I have included in my amendment to the amendment a matter having to do with the taxation field. The letter that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) tabled the other day contained new proposals having to do with taxation under which the provinces were to get 10 per cent of the income tax, 9 per cent of an unstated corporation tax, and 50 cents out of every dollar of succession duty. The objective is certainly a good one, namely, to bring the tax income of the poorer provinces up to that of the richer provinces. However, I would have the house recognize that the richer provinces are relinquishing the three major fields of taxation on a rental basis. If those provinces are to continue to produce and develop their resources and to be in a position to keep pouring dollars into the coffers of the federal government, then it will be necessary for them to receive more income to keep the rest of Canada happy.
In my province we would have no objection to assisting those other provinces, if we felt for a moment that the federal authorities were not, through their bungling and interfering methods, ruining the chances of some of those other provinces of advancing. Let me take our own case. In British Columbia last year we had an instance of the federal authorities interfering with our river development, as proposed by the government of British Columbia. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), as well as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage), thought that we should divert water from the Columbia river into the Fraser. Because the Columbia river would come under the authority of the federal government, it left only one river over which the provincial government would have authority, namely, the Fraser river.

This was not the only instance of interference in our province or in any other province. Mr. Speaker, at the start of this important session, while we are on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, will you kindly allow me to join the other members of the house in offering my best wishes to you and in pointing out how able and dignified has been


your chairmanship of the proceedings of this Canadian parliament. You bring to the discharge of these difficult duties remarkable tact and fairness. Your knowledge of parliamentary law and of the rules of the house, and more particularly the way in which you apply them in practice, place you in the first rank of the eminent Canadians who have preceded you in the Speaker's chair.
My most sincere good wishes also go to the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) whose magnificent good health and fruitful labour are such as to forecast more happy and prosperous days for the whole Canadian people.
May I also heartily congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address (Mrs. Shipley and Mr. Laflamme). Their constituents may rightly be satisfied with them and must be proud, after seeing them at work, of having asked them to represent their constituencies in the parliament of the nation.
I rise today, Mr. Speaker, because I feel it is my duty to submit to the house and to the members of government a few practical suggestions, a few constructive ideas which, to my mind, are likely to help my electors and those of all constituencies of the country.
I must first express regret at the absence in the speech from the throne of any indication of the government's intention to propose, at this session, health insurance legislation, a measure which would add to the impressive body of social security legislation put forward by representatives of the Liberal party in recent years and later adopted by parliament. I know the feelings of the right hon. Prime Minister on the matter. I know that the members of his cabinet understand the urgency and necessity of this essential measure, that already they have long debated its advantages and foreseen the difficulty of putting it into force.
The question of a health insurance plan has been discussed in Canada for a long time.
I believe that the time has come to put the project into effect so that our people may without further delay benefit from this salutary legislation. We have now come to the point where something must be done to protect the large number of our fellow citizens who are suddenly taken sick.
When a child or a mother is sick, the cost of medical and hospital care may be heavy, but when sickness suddenly strikes the father, the head of the family, the cost of the necessary care becomes almost prohibitive. There is no use in trying to hide the truth, Mr. Speaker; at present, in a country that enjoys

Canada's prosperity, only two classes of people are in a position to get the necessary care, the needy and the rich. People who come under the public assistance act, or those who are personally well off can afford the luxury of going to the hospital. There is no alternative. As for the average Canadian, the middle class man, the one we usually call the white-collar worker, the man who has a small income, who is on a fixed salary-and that group includes the great majority of our workers and farmers-is no longer able to pay alone the cost of medical, surgical and hospital care. This fact cannot be challenged. The farsighted head of a family who has painstakingly managed to put a few dollars away for a rainy day is ruthlessly ruined when illness strikes him or anyone in his family. A few weeks in hospital and his property is mortgaged, his savings gone and he must then ask for credit and borrow money often at prohibitive rates.
Every day some good people come to my office to ask for assistance, because they cannot afford to pay their hospital bills, or those of the doctor, the surgeon or even the druggist. Hundreds of others, as I have just said, fall prey to lending institutions and have to pay interest up to 24 per cent to fill the gap left by a recent illness.
Some time ago, a respectable man whom I know very well and with whom I have been associated, a man of temperate habits, in other words a man like the hundreds of thousands of others in this country, came to me to tell of his sad experience. Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to repeat this story to my colleagues as it shows the necessity of a protecting health insurance legislation, of an immediate, well drafted and truly generous act, one which, if I may say so incidentally, will allow the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) to convince his colleague, the member for Three Rivers in the Quebec legislative assembly, to co-operate for once for the general welfare of the population. He must know or rather we know that, by itself, the federal government can do nothing in that field; it has to rely on the full co-operation of all the provincial governments without exception. After this little digression I now turn to my story.
Last fall, an honest man whom I have known since childhood, a man of 60 who has worked all his life and has managed to save some $8,000-you will admit that $8,000 is
The Address-Mr. Gingues not very much but it is a rather considerable amount for a man who earns a modest salary and has to save this money bit by bit-came to my office. Two years ago, his wife was taken ill. She was taken to the hospital where she underwent an operation. She was in and out of the hospital for a period of two years. He came to my office, crying like a child, to tell me that in the short period of two years all the money he had saved in order to have some security in his old age was gone, and that he was now sick himself and could no longer do his usual work. Well, Mr. Speaker, this would mean that, at 60, this man who is still young, will be unable to obtain the old age pension and will be forced, owing to sickness, to depend on public relief.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a special case, but I could mention many others which strangely resemble this one.
That is why I say, at the beginning of this 1956 session, that the time has come to enact legislation in that field.
I know that certain doctors, certain specialists-not all, fortunately-fear the inroads of health insurance legislation. Still, to my mind, the common good must prevail over particular interests. I am speaking here today in this house, on behalf of the community as a whole. When anything has become a national scourge the duty of the lawmakers is to take whatever means are necessary to set matters right.
The one and only means, in this case, is federal legislation supported by similar provincial legislation.
This measure has become necessary, I repeat, not because our hospitals abuse their privileges and overcharge their patients. That is not the case. In hospitals, as everywhere else, everything is more expensive and like all well organized corporations they have to balance their budget. However, when this law is assented to, the very great majority of Canadians who, I repeat, earn enough to live from day to day but hardly enough to make any savings, even when they are in perfect health, will feel they are protected and will enjoy thereby a greater feeling of security. If anything should happen to them, their morale will remain good and their chances of getting well again will be better. Under the present system there are large numbers of poor people who have to shorten their period of

The Address-Mr. Gingues convalescence so as to reduce costs and who undergo serious relapses a short time later.
I know that thousands of sick people go back to work too soon because that is their only means of earning a livelihood for their family. Hence the great number of premature deaths in these families, because the last link in the chain of social security legislation given the country by the Liberal party has not yet been welded.
Since my election to this house in 1940, I have had the pleasure to vote for great social enactments of this government. First, it was the marvellous Family Allowances Act, then the Unemployment Insurance Act, the amendments to the Old Age Security Act, to the Blind Persons Act and to the Disabled Persons Act. I was happy then to advocate and support these basically Liberal measures. I shall be happier still, Mr. Speaker, to vote for a health insurance act for, if there is in life a time when we need help and the solace of human fraternity, it is when illness strikes us and when misfortune knocks at our door. I shall not insist any more, because I know all my colleagues share this feeling.

Mr. Speaker, last week, when I was listening to my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Brown), my speech was all prepared in French. When I heard him address himself to the house in my maternal tongue, and this for quite a few minutes, I decided to do likewise, and that is why I shall continue a part of my remarks in English. I hope that effort of my hon. friend and mine at this moment will contribute to good understanding amongst us members.
There is another suggestion which I would like to submit to the government, and particularly to the Minister of Finance. I should rather say two suggestions, because the matter with which I wish to deal concerns both the budget and the income tax.
In income tax return forms there is an item dealing with charitable donations made by every individual, by every taxpayer during the year. It is stated therein that a maximum of 10 per cent of the net income may be deducted for that purpose. In order to benefit from these exemptions, one must attach to the income tax reports receipts signed by charitable organizations, members of the clergy or other authorized persons. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this entails additional inconveniences for the taxpayer. He


is not only compelled to figure out his income to the last cent, but he must endeavour to obtain a receipt which will justify, so to speak, a great number of small or negligible donations, the amount of which is rather difficult to remember. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that all this paper work be done away with and that these proceedings be simplified by putting everyone on the same footing, that is, by simply allowing everyone a 10 per cent deduction of net income for charitable donations.
This is the practice in other countries. Why should we not do the same in Canada? This would simplify matters and would be fairer to the taxpayer and easier for the income tax department. I therefore request the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to include this amendment or improvement in his next budget. I believe everyone will benefit therefrom.
And since I am talking about the budget, I should like to put before the Minister of Finance another request, and a very important one, the immediate granting of which could bring about happy results. By this, Mr. Speaker, I mean that the national budget should be presented sooner. I believe that the budget should be presented to the house in January every year, and I shall tell you why. Most merchants, industrialists and businessmen take inventory after the festive season, that is, at the beginning of January. After that they must wait weeks and even months before finding out whether changes will be made in the Customs Act, Excise Tax Act, the sales tax or otherwise.
Owing to this state of uncertainty most merchants wait before making purchases, and I believe that this situation is greatly responsible for the increase in seasonal unemployment which occurs mostly during the months of January, February, March and April. The unemployment insurance commission, together with municipalities, chambers of commerce and other public bodies, and also individuals, are doing constructive work in order to alleviate this idle period which we call seasonal unemployment. If the budget were presented in January I believe this situation would not be as bad.
I am asking the Minister of Finance to study this matter carefully. We would indeed be entirely justified to act accordingly if thousands of workers could be retained in their jobs who otherwise must rely for their livelihood on their unemployment insurance benefits. I would be curious to find out the opinion of merchants and manufacturers about this scheme.
After submitting these suggestions, which I believe are in the general interest of all

Canadians, may I, Mr. Speaker, put forward a request which concerns especially my district, the eastern townships. I am asking this now of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-ler), whose sympathetic disposition we all know. In Quebec, as you know, the eastern townships are a small province within a province, and Sherbrooke, which I am privileged to represent in the house, is its capital. Writers and poets compare Sherbrooke to a queen and certain neighbouring towns to pearls and other jewels. They are right because Providence has showered its favours upon this privileged district which is represented by a dozen members in this house. We have rich mines, a great variety of industries; our population is progressive and alert, we have wonderful agricultural domains, an attractive countryside, magnificent mountains, large lakes teeming with fish, excellent hunting grounds, a prosperous tourist industry; in other words, prospects for a most brilliant future.
We also have numerous land transport facilities. The eastern townships are served by the large railways, the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and the Quebec Central which runs from Sherbrooke to Quebec City, via the rich mining district of Thetford Mines and Black Lake. We have numerous highways which, of course, could be improved but nevertheless help in expanding trade and industry. However, something is lacking. The eastern townships need air services which would speed up transportation between Sherbrooke, Quebec city and Montreal, and consequently with the rest of the world.
The minister knows that strong representations were made to his department for the building of an airport near Sherbrooke. Trans-Canada Air Lines were approached and, if I am not mistaken, they are making a survey at the present time of the passenger potentialities which the eastern townships would offer. I do not want to prophesy, but I can assert that air lines which would call at Sherbrooke would find it to their financial advantage.
As I have already said, the population of the eastern townships is progressive and full of initiative. They do not like to be behind the times. But in the field of air communications we are lagging behind other districts in our province and in the rest of the country. Therefore I request the Minister of Transport to provide in his 1956 budget sufficient estimates for the construction of at least two runways at the St. Frangois airport, a few miles from Sherbrooke. In asking him to act as soon as possible, I am talking not only on behalf of the citizens of Sherbrooke but also on behalf of the population of the whole district.
The Address-Mr. W. M. Hamilton
I am convinced that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who is one of the most illustrious sons of the eastern townships, will support my request with his colleague and that when I go back to Sherbrooke I will be able to assure my constituents that the airport for which we have been waiting for such a long time will be built this year.

When we rose for lunch, Mr. Speaker, I was just about to make a comparison between the care of money and other valuables as taken by the post office and by the banks, in an attempt to show that many of the thefts from the post office are the direct result of inefficiency and lack of attention on the part of

the senior administrators of the department. I think an example is best drawn from a situation which arose last December in Cha-teauguay. I hold in my hand a newspaper clipping with photographs from the Gazette of Thursday, December 22. I am reading the caption of that picture which summarizes the situation fairly well:
When Miss Marie Soyer, daughter of Chateauguay Mayor George Soyer and post office clerk for the town, entered her office yesterday morning she saw a scene of wreckage and looting. The post office was robbed of $500 in stamps and $49 in cash when thieves smashed the lock on a box. But when the burglars attempted to loot the Banque Canadienne Nationale bank safe in the building they faced a different proposition. After drilling through the left side of the vault for at least six inches, they were forced to call a halt when they hit a solid sheet of cold steel.
Here, we have a situation in which a post office and the branch of a bank in the same building are entered on the same day. The post office is looted but the bank property remains safe. Someone listening to these words, and thinking in terms of the great banks of our larger cities, might think that the bank had an almost impenetrable vault. The interesting thing is that this clipping contains a photograph of this particular vault. We find it is an ordinary office safe, about four feet high, such as one will find in office after office across this country and costing a comparatively few dollars in relation to the valuables which it contains. It is the sort of thing one would expect a post office, when they have $500 or $1,000-in some cases $20,000-worth of valuables to have.
What do we find in this instance, and doubtless in instance after instance across the country? If the valuables are put away at all they are put away in a box, something that thieves could break open and remove the contents with a minimum of difficulty. If these thefts were only isolated around the country, perhaps we would have no major cause for worry. But the pattern as was shown last year, and the pattern that has continued to evolve month after month as is evidenced by newspaper story after newspaper story, is that the post office is considered, shall we say, a good business proposition for thieves. For some reason, almost certainly the lack of protection the post office is giving to the valuables it has, these thieves are breaking into post office after post office.

I should think, however, that they would not assist in such an investigation. The detection of crime in a province is under the jurisdiction of the provincial police and it would be only in the event of their calling in the mounted police or the post office calling in the mounted police that the mounted police would act.
In the last few days we have seen a most considerable mess in the government benches, with the ministers not knowing what they were answering and with contradictions between one another, so this should come as no surprise. Let me emphasize that here again, on the same day within a few minutes of one another, you have the Prime Minister of this country saying there is very close co-operation between the R.C.M.P. and the post office, and the R.C.M.P. are working on these matters. Then we have the Minister of Justice under whom the R.C.M.P. comes, stating he does not think they would be called in on a particular case. It is for that reason I suggest that the present investigatory staff of the post office, which, according to the estimates of last year, numbers five people, might very well be transferred to the jurisdiction of the R.C.M.P. Certainly the R.C.M.P. should be given final and absolute responsibility, in so far as federal jurisdiction is concerned, for the protection of Her

The Address-Mr. W. M. Hamilton Majesty's mails. I feel that if that were done this fine national police force we have would make considerable progress in a field which has so far given us nothing but a cause for worry.
Turning to another aspect of the post office service I should like to ask again, as I did last year, that the post office consider the re-establishment of the two-a-day mail delivery rather than the present one-a-day system which extends into such a large part of Canada. We should have a two-a-day mail delivery on a five-day week basis.
The immediate objection raised by the post office to the return to the two-a-day mail delivery is the increase in the cost. As one who has discussed this thing, not only with some of the biased people in Ottawa, but with people on the lower levels right across the country, I would point out that the return to the two-a-day, five days a week delivery would not cause a major cost increase in the operation of the post office.
Some people may ask, why can we not have mail delivered twice a day on a six-day basis? I would point out to them that the great majority of the industrial concerns of this country even our banks and other businesses, are now on a five-day week basis, and that from a realistic point of view it would be better to have ten deliveries a week than the existing one delivery a day for six days.
My second point is that such a system would eliminate a great deal of the difficulties -now arising in mail delivery across the country. Under the present system, in order to arrange for delivery six days a week, the post office must employ a man for one of those six days who is unfamiliar with the route, and who rotates from route to route, spending only one day a week on each route. That enables them to have a five-day week for their employees. However, mail service is a very personal thing. All the myriad little changes which occur on a route are not known to those rotating mail carriers, or supervisory letter carriers, as the technical term is. The result is, there are continual complaints, continual difficulties and continual embarrassments for the post office.
Under a five-day-a-week system, the same man would service his route continuously, and the service to the people of that route would be improved as the number of complaints would be reduced. Another great advantage of this, Mr. Speaker, would be that the system would eliminate the miserable unfairness which the post office has instituted for most of its letter carriers on the island of Montreal. Unlike the rest of Canada where seniority is given primary consideration in


establishing summer vacations for letter carriers, another factor has entered into the picture in Montreal, and that has moved supervisory letter carriers of comparatively few years' experience ahead of men with many years of experience on the vacation lists. If this were being done across Canada on an equal basis the post office might perhaps claim that there was some reason for it and that it was necessary, -but it has been instituted in only a very few centres in Canada. In Toronto they have a totally different system of establishing the vacation period. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this inequity should be remedied. We tried to get that done last year and we were unsuccessful. The reason given was that it was brought up just as the vacation schedules were being established. Well, this year, slow moving as the department is, and slow moving as the minister may be, we at least have sufficient time for him to make up his mind and do something about this particular situation.
Let me turn now to a few things of local interest in Montreal. I should like to join my voice to that of the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau), when he gets around to it, in suggesting that there be an underpass constructed, and that very shortly, on Decarie boulevard, north of the Cote de Liesse traffic circle. That is a major traffic artery in the city. It presents a considerable danger, with trains periodically travelling across it. It is the wish of the people of that area that something be done about it and before too long.
I could not help but be amused by the typical example of this government's operation which I saw not too long ago in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway. I am delighted to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) in the house at this time. The seaway, of course, is well under way. We have already poured out millions upon millions of dollars into the construction, and now we are going to make models of it. I have no doubt that the models may serve a purpose. It is not the models that I object to so much, Mr. Speaker, as the basis on which we are going to house them. In the Globe and Mail of Toronto of December 6 we find this:
The seaway authority also announced that a $500,000 contract has been awarded for the construction of two models of the seaway sections in the Montreal area.
Further on we find this:
The contract calls for the construction of a $300,000 building to house the models. The models will cost an estimated $120,000.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, they are going to have a building to house a model which is two and one-half times the value of the

model, a model of something which is already well on its way to completion. There is very grave doubt in my mind of the necessity for such a building, particularly even if we admit the need for the model.
The other day I listened with a great deal of interest to the comments of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on the question of wheat and agriculture. I must say that after having travelled across this great country of ours not more than a couple of months ago from Winnipeg through to Vancouver and back, and after having listened to many people in that area, I came to the conclusion that the government has a certain policy on wheat and on agriculture. I have come to the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that it is a two-part policy. It is compounded in equal parts of faith in the Liberal party and hope for a crop failure. As far as I have been able to see, that is about the only helpful advice or counsel that the government has so far been able to put forward in connection with the wheat surplus.
I do hope that when the estimates come down later this year we shall be able to get an explanation of some of the items in the public accounts book which reached us recently. The attention of hon. members should be drawn particularly to this book because there is so much of interest in it. I looked at a little item in the book only this morning and I discovered that one gentleman had drawn something over $11,000 in travelling expenses in the year ended March 31, 1955, and another gentleman had drawn something over $7,800 in travelling expenses. Both of these gentlemen are in the Department of Transport. I am reasonably sure that in the one case there is an explanation, but it is interesting to note that that explanation was brought forth by questioning by myself in the house last year. I believe the department has changed its policy in this regard.
This gentleman drew $11,000 in travelling expenses but what actually happened in that particular case is that he had a number of people working for him and he put in for their travelling expenses as well as for his own and apparently disbursed the money back to them. That policy I am informed has now been changed as a result of the representations made last year.
Let me point out that it was not until this matter was brought up in the house and the government criticized on that particular point that anything was done about an employee of the government disbursing funds to other employees. Eleven thousand dollars is a sizeable amount of money to give to any one individual to use to pay the travelling expenses of other people.

I am not at all sure that the same explanation applies to the other case which will be found on Z-84 of the public accounts. In that case the man received $7,865 in travelling expenses last year. I look forward with considerable interest to an explanation of that case.
When selecting people for government service there seems to be a practice on the part of the government to insist on abnormally high qualifications for particular jobs. Let me say at once that properly trained, properly educated, properly prepared people are necessary for many of the posts in our government, but at the same time let me say that there are many jobs which do not require a university degree as a qualification. Individual cases should be examined on their merits. Let me show what the government is doing in certain cases.
I have here an advertisement for fire protection officers, whose duties will be, under the supervision of the dominion fire commissioner, to inspect, test and report upon the condition of fire protection facilities n. 'uding chemical extinguishers, stand pipes ann hose systems, automatic sprinkler systems and the like. We have all seen this type of man who occupies a most important position going up and down the corridors of important buildings checking the fire extinguishers to see that they are in operating shape.
The desirable qualifications given for this position include graduation from a university of recognized standing in science, majoring in mathematics, physics and chemistry with preference being given to applicants with at least one year of experience in fire prevention or related work with boards of insurance underwriters, and so on.
One hardly needs a man with a university degree to go around checking fire extinguishers, stand pipes and automatic sprinkler systems. I make that statement with the proviso always that we must have people who have adequate training, adequate education and so on to fit them for the particular job they are going to do.

speechtext:
As
someone says, "And be a Liberal." More and more one wonders whether these specifications are drawn up with someone specially in mind. I do not know that and I do not suggest that. This is not a matter of sour grapes as I am a university graduate. I feel most keenly that university training is required in many positions, but I am open-minded enough about it to realize that there are many positions to fill in this country where that sort of experience and education is not required. The quickest way to make a person unhappy is to take a man of superior education and perhaps intellectual attainments and put him at checking fire extinguishers in a government building and setting rat traps. It seems to me essentially that is what the government is trying to do in these two cases and I bring them forward for your consideration.
A matter which is causing considerable concern in Montreal has to do with the

Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). Our hope is that he will consider amending the Criminal Code to cover the operation of private card houses. As I understand it, at the present time the Criminal Code legalizes the operation of a room or club where for the payment of 10 cents an hour or 50 cents a day people may play cards or gamble legally. It seems to me that this should be corrected. When that section was included in the Criminal Code 50 cents a day or 10 cents an hour were realistic amounts, but the cost of everything has gone up and this section should be corrected on that ground alone quite apart from the inconvenience and trouble it is causing the Montreal police department at the present time in proving cases against people.
I want to express the hope that this year those members of the government who occupy the treasury benches will keep their noses to the grindstone and stay with us in this house. Some of them are quite good about it but others are a little bit delinquent. I am not only thinking of the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) who went off salmon fishing last year when his bill was up in the house.
I do want to express my regret at one particular instance. In the heat of last summer, when we here were doing our very best, I read in the newspaper that a certain cabinet minister had arrived in London for a two-week vacation. It so happened that during the course of that vacation his estimates were considered in the house and were quite ably handled by another minister. I am not going to name the particular minister, as I think it would be a little unfair to him, but this illustrates an approach to this house and to the nation's business that, in my opinion, is very strongly to be condemned. That is only one illustration of their disregard for their responsibilities and disregard for the work of this house, and it could be multiplied many times.
I should like to mention just one final point, since I see I have a moment for it. Earlier in this speech, I gave an illustration of the confusion existing between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice regarding what the R.C.M.P. and the Post Office Department were doing. I wish the departments would get themselves at least halfway sorted out. I have here an advertisement by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration for an architect with several years' varied experience to help with all types of buildings for Indian agencies and reserves across Canada. We all know that the primary responsibility of the Department of Public Works is in that

field, but now we find that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has to have its own officer.
Then we find that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is looking for an engineer to be responsible for certain installations in the Jasper national park. On the other hand, the Department of Public Works is looking for two engineers to take care of highways in the national parks. In other words, these departments, in the confusion which is so rampant in the government, are running one over the other willynilly. Without any consideration for the taxpayers, without any consideration for expenditures, without any consideration for anything except building their own private empires, these ministers, one after the other, are advertising for people, and in many cases they do not even know what to do with them.
I am quite sure that, when the estimates come up for consideration this year, we shall be able to look at some of these situations, and we shall certainly give the government every possible help we can in straightening out the stupid mess it is getting itself into today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to offer my congratulations, as previous speakers have done, to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley) on the very fine way in which she moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Timiskaming is one of the outstanding women of today. She was outstanding in her own riding before she came to this house and she has certainly been an asset to all of us here and a credit to the women of Canada. I am quite sure that her appeal to the Prime Minister to appoint a woman to sit on the civil service commission will not fall upon deaf ears.
I should like also to congratulate the seconder of the motion, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Laflamme). His fine oratory and his knowledge of parliamentary business were very apparent, and we certainly welcome him to this corner of the house.
The matter about which I intend to speak today is, to my mind, of very urgent public importance. I had intended to discuss it when the estimates relating to the Department of Justice were before the house but events over the past four weeks have been of such a serious and critical nature that I must bring it to the attention of the Minister of Justice and the hon. members of this house at this time.
The city of Hamilton, in which I have the honour to represent the riding of Hamilton
The Address-Mr. Reinke South, is, I believe, an average Canadian city. One of my hon. friends says it is a little better than average, and I agree with him. In the space of a few more years it will no doubt reach a population of a quarter of a million people, since we are now fast approaching that population. The people of Hamilton, as I have said, are average people; they are hard-working, industrious, peace-loving citizens fulfilling their duties to their families and to their communities.
I point out this fact because what I am about to say affects the citizens of every town and city across this great dominion of ours. Whilst I am going to refer to my own particular riding, it is only because I am more cognizant of conditions there than I am of any other communities across Canada.
The people of our municipality are incensed, the citizens are riled, they are desperate and they are afraid. The men are afraid for the safety of their wives, and parents for their daughters. Why are they afraid? Because we have never in the history of our city experienced a more serious and! despicable wave of heinous sex crimes than at the present time. Since December 5, eight cases of sexual assault have been reported to the police. Of these assaults reported, five have been brutal cases of rape.
Last Friday night a small young mother of a young child was hauled into a car as she walked along the street in the west central part of the city. She was taken to the outskirts of the city, was attacked by two men who were in the car, and was turned loose to wander about in a dazed condition until she finally reached a telephone. Since that time, an 18-year-old girl was abducted by two men, badly beaten, taken to a motel on the outskirts of town and there assaulted by one of the men.
Last Monday night, a 52-year-old woman complained to the city police that she had been raped by two men on a lonely township road just outside the city limits.
The week end before Christmas, a young couple walking home from a dance were assaulted by two men. The husband was knocked to the ground partially unconscious. His terrified wife was pulled into a car, assaulted and left near a small town on the outskirts of Hamilton.
Just two weeks ago, a 15-year-old girl on her way home from a skating rink in the east end of the city suffered a similar fate. On Sunday morning, a daring daylight attempt was made by two men on a 25-year-old girl. Here it is reported in the Hamilton. Spectator of Tuesday, 17th January:
The attacks have resulted in strict security regulations being put into effect at the student nurses' residence at St. Joseph's hospital. Girls

The Address-Mr. Reinke are not being allowed out alone at night and all late passes have been cancelled for the time, it was learned today.
Many parents are taking the precaution of driving their daughters to and from places at night until the case is cleared up.
Then we have another account on the following evening, Wednesday, 18th January. The Spectator for that date contains the following report:
One of those "barbaric rapists" who have been terrorizing young women in the Hamilton district recently could be that young man who lives next door! If you're hunting for the $3,000 reward money offered for their arrest don't assume that the wanted pair are thuggish "bums" from the underworld. You have the word of their latest victim, the attractive young woman who was attacked in broad daylight at Aberdeen and James streets Tuesday, that they are not.
"That's the surprising part of it," she told the Spectator this morning. "The man who grabbed me seemed like a Quite ordinary young man."
"You mean he looked quite respectable?"
"Yes, he did. He was neat and clean. There was nothing untidy or dirty about him."
I have no doubt whatsoever, Mr. Speaker, that the police of Hamilton will apprehend these thugs. Four of these attacks have taken the same pattern and are attributed to the same men. But what will we do with these callous, hardened beasts, once they are apprehended? What will happen to the degenerate who murdered 5-year-old Susan Cadieux of London, who after this despicable crime left her to die of exposure? What will happen to the sadistic rapist who spirited away 13-year-old Linda Lampkin of Toronto Wednesday night, strangled her with her own scarf and, according to newspaper reports, threw her battered body from a moving vehicle on Commissioner street in Toronto?
Most people are not aware, however, that the biggest percentage of these degenerates are sane. To back up that statement I should like to read the opinion of the superintendent of a mental hospital as reported in the Hamilton Spectator of Tuesday, January 17, which is as follows:
Dr. J. N. Senn, superintendent of the Ontario hospital here, said today the majority of suspected sex offenders committed by magistrates for observation are returned to the courts as sane persons.
I am not in a position to criticize the punishments or penalties handed out by our courts, but I will say that either our Criminal Code should be made more stringent or it is not being enforced severely enough, and I am inclined to lean towards the latter view. Section 136 of the Criminal Code reads:
Every one who commits rape is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life and to be whipped.
I think this section is perfectly clear. I believe every man who commits this offence 
should receive the maximum penalty. He should be put out of society for all time and be given lashes. Section 137 reads as follows:
Every one who attempts to commit rape is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for ten years and to be whipped.
Here again I suggest that every offender should receive the maximum penalty. These people deserve no sympathy. I am speaking now of course of the sane person who wilfully and methodically sets out to carry out this act. As I have pointed out from good authority, I believe most of them come under this category no matter how they may try to hide behind the curtain of insanity. The penalty is there and must be meted out severely to act as a deterrent to others.
But more dangerous perhaps than the type of criminals I have just mentioned, who have been molesting women and children in Hamilton, is the type of sex deviate involved in the last two instances I referred to, the Cadieux case in London and the Lampkin case in Toronto. This is the type of criminal who, after committing this foul deed, kills his victim for the purpose, I suppose, of hiding his identity. The Hon. Kelso Roberts, attorney general of Ontario, expressed his views in the Toronto Star of January 12, 1956, as follows:
We are concerned about these cases and we are studying the problem but we have got to move slowly. I sympathize with the people who are angry over these recent assaults on children. But we cannot just go around locking up each and every sex deviate. We are not behind the iron curtain. We have got to try and understand each individual problem.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I most vehemently oppose this opinion. I should like to know why in heaven's name we cannot lock up each and every sex deviate. To my mind any man who is guilty of molesting small girls or full grown ones, for that matter, is a sex deviate. Under section 661 of the Criminal Code these men can be taken out of society for an indeterminate period and for life if necessary. I suggest that if the act of molesting, which in effect is an indecent assault, takes place more than once, society should be rid of that person at least until this complex problem is solved and while it is being solved.
To me it would seem reasonable to assume that the sex deviate probably begins his life of crime in the same way as a bandit or an alcoholic. It is very unlikely that a thief would attempt to rob the main branch of the Royal Bank of Canada in Ottawa in his first attempt at crime. I cannot conceive of a person becoming an alcoholic after one drink. It is a state that is brought into being progressively as the person becomes

bolder and bolder and more irresponsible, gradually acquiring a thirst that cannot be quenched. The same is true of the sex deviate. His first offence may be to watch little children playing in the grounds of a school and attempt to entice them away. Becoming bolder and bolder and taking fewer precautions, he is finally successful in luring them to their downfall and leaving them maimed for life or ravaged and killed.
If life imprisonment and the lash are not enough of a deterrent, then these crimes must be prevented before they happen by taking these molesters out of circulation. I maintain that these men, who are urged by some mental deviation to molest children, even though it may be in a minor way at first, should be held in custody, and if they have not been guilty of indecent assault under section 141, which deals with that crime, we should add another section to this part of the code to deal with those who begin with a minor sex offence. One thing I am certain of is that we must be strict in dealing with these men.
I am pleased that at last we have section 162 dealing with peeping Toms. You have no doubt read of sex crimes committed by criminals who started by peeping in a window of an apartment or a home. The first thing you know some urge impels them to gain entry and then there is an assault and possibly a murder.
Some five years ago I had a personal experience in this connection. We were preparing for bed one evening and our dog kicked up quite a racket. I threw on my dressing gown quickly and went out to investigate. I arrived in time to see someone jumping over the side fence and then run around the side of the house next door and out to the street. A few hundred feet up the street a car was parked. Of course I was not attired to take chase but I got the colour and make of the car and so on and telephoned the police.
While I was waiting for the police to come I jumped in my own car to see if I could spot the car in the district. I noticed the car as a matter of fact cruising the district about two blocks away but unfortunately I was travelling the wrong way when I spotted it and by the time I had turned around he had disappeared. I returned to my home and waited for the arrival of the police. I was standing on the front verandah still attired in my dressing gown and, lo and behold, I looked over on the next street and saw what appeared to be someone looking in a window. I thought: How could this be so soon after this has happened to me?
The Address-Mr. Reinke
I went into the house, secured a flashlight and turned it on this house which faced the same way mine did but was on the next block. There framed against a back window was this fellow looking in a bedroom. Of course he immediately noticed the light on him and took off with me after him. Here I was still only in my dressing gown. He ran down the block a hundred yards or so and I think I was gaining on him a little. I was younger in those days and in better shape. He jumped in his car and fled.
But this time I was fortunate enough to secure the licence number, so I turned it over to the police and he was apprehended. My wife and I picked him out of a line-up the next day, and sure enough it was he. He came from a good, respectable family in Hamilton, and was married and had two or three children. As a matter of fact, I felt sorry for him. He having pleaded guilty to this offence, the judge said, "I am powerless to convict him", and he was let off on suspended sentence. Of course at that time the code contained no provision for this type of crime. He was let off, put on a $100 bond and I think for a period of two years he was to stay out of that district. That was all the satisfaction that I had after this man came to my own window and within half an hour was looking into the window of someone across the street.
Let me read to you, Mr. Speaker, the definition of a criminal sexual psychopath as defined in our Criminal Code under section 659:
. . . (b) "criminal sexual psychopath" means a person who, by a course of misconduct in sexual matters, has shown a lack of power to control his sexual impulses and who as a result is likely to attack-
I would ask you to note those words "likely to attack".
-or otherwise inflict injury, pain or other evil on any person, . . .
Then it goes on and points out that preventive detention under the act means detention in a penitentiary for an indeterminate period. Are these men not criminal sexual psychopaths? Either they go back into society completely cured or they should stay in prison or in a mental institution. Whether they can be cured without surgery is not for me to say, since I am not a psychiatrist nor a doctor. In a great many cases I am of the opinion that surgery may be the answer. Those who are opposed to this solution might do well to remember the words of our Lord when He delivered His sermon
368	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy on the mount as is written in the gospel according to St. Matthew, dealing with adultery:
29.	And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
30.	And if thy right hand offend thee, cut It off, and cast it from thee: . . .
And so on. A royal commission, headed by Chief Justice McRuer, is studying the problem to see whether the section of the Criminal Code dealing with sex offences should be changed. That commission is holding meetings and has been sitting for two years in all parts of Canada. I would certainly hope that the commission will report to parliament at this session so that we shall have an opportunity to see whether this part of the Criminal Code needs some revising. Our children must come first. We are not going to keep them locked up or under surveillance while this sort of deviate runs at large.
Since 1947 when section 661 of the code was passed by parliament-that is the section to which I just referred-only 20 men in all of Canada have been given indeterminate sentences under this section dealing with sexual psychopaths. Possibly this is because sex offences are seldom repeated after the criminal has paid his penalty. Of 5,821 cases studied in New York city, 39 per cent had previous police records but for other offences. Only 9 per cent had been involved in previous sex offences. If our percentages in this country are comparable, surely 9 per cent of the sex deviates would amount to more than 20 over the past eight years. I can therefore only conclude that although under our Criminal Code we have provided a law under which to commit these men, our courts have been too lenient. This 9 per cent must be securely placed in detention forever or until there is no chance of recurrence, so that mothers and their daughters can once more move about without any fear whether it be daylight or dark.
