speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to join those members who have preceded me in offering my congratulations to the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and the seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The mover of the address, namely the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley), can, with considerable justification, feel proud of the fact that she is the first woman in Canada to have had that honour. What I think may be of equal importance to her as a Liberal as well as a woman is the fact that at long


last the Liberal party have succeeded in electing a woman upon whom they can bestow that high honour.
Those of us who have been here for some years, Mr. Speaker, do not expect to find much by way of progressive legislation or of new legislation proposed in the speech from the throne in the third session of a parliament with an election more than a year away. The best we can hope for is a vague foreshadowing of better things to come when election year comes around, possibly next session. It is therefore gratifying to find in the speech from the throne a promise of legislation to provide, as between men and women, equal pay for equal work in the federal section of our economy. This is a matter for which another lady member of the house, namely the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough), will be justified in taking some credit.
It would really be interesting if we were to make a study of just how much of the Liberal legislation introduced over the past years has originated on this side of the house. I think a close study would reveal the fact that most if not all of the best legislation that has been introduced by this government in the past 20 years or so was first brought to the attention of the house and the country by one or other of the opposition groups. As a matter of fact, it looks very much as though the government no longer takes the initiative or leadership in the field of progressive legislation but rather has become the agent of the opposition to implement legislation proposed by opposition groups.
Now that we have voted on the question of wheat surpluses it may be well to look at some of the other major issues that confront us today. First and foremost among those, in my opinion, is the international relationship between east and west, that which we speak of as the tension between east and west which exists at the present time. I refer to the struggle for supremacy between the communists and the capitalist countries of the world. It is the struggle for supremacy between Russia and her allies on the one side and the United States and her allies on the other. It is an issue, Mr. Speaker, the outcome of which is a matter of life and death for a whole generation of people in every country in the world today.
We can talk all we like about peaceful coexistence or competitive coexistence, but I think the cold stark fact is that as long as we have communism and capitalism dividing the world with two ideologies that struggle for supremacy will continue. The most we can probably hope for in the years to come is that the contest can be carried on without

recourse to war. In view of the situation, it seems to me we should direct our thoughts along two main lines. We should first of all seek to use all the prestige and influence that Canada can command amongst the nations of the world to avoid what Mr. Eden has chosen to call a universal explosion. Secondly, we should seek to find ways and means of demonstrating to our own people, and to the people of other nations, nations that are now teetering in their support between the east and the west, that the democratic way of life can provide more tangible benefits than can the communist way of life. As I see it, that is the twofold challenge which confronts both the governments and the citizens of the countries of the free world today.
Mr. Eden was reported in the press yesterday as having pledged the British people to keep working for some way in which the communist nations and the free world can live together without quarrelling over the domination of the world. Canada has good reason to be proud of the prominent part which our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and our Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) have played in this field. I think Canadians everywhere recognize and congratulate those ministers on the good job they did for Canada and the world during recent months. Even though there are new clouds on the horizon, even though there may be new problems arising every day, we must, to use the words of our own Secretary of State for External Affairs-
-stand firm against tactics of divide, weaken and destroy, but equally do nothing by provocative word or policy to increase Russia's fear of the west as a threat to peace.
While we welcome those words from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, we wonder how the policy of the government which has recently come to light regarding the shipment of arms to Egypt can be made to fit in with the secretary's words. It would seem that there really does exist a right and a left in government circles, and that the government's right hand does not really know what the left hand is doing nor the left what the right is doing. We have heard a great deal of criticism regarding Russia's or the communist countries' shipments of arms to Egypt in recent months. One wonders just why we can blame one country for shipping these arms while we are engaged in the same practice.
So, Mr. Speaker, defence and negotiation must continue hand in hand. While we give our support to measures of protection against communism, we must continue our efforts to secure a genuine disarmament agreement. I want to add my voice to others in urging
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy the government, and particularly the two ministers already referred to, to continue persevering to secure such an agreement. Here, I want to call attention to the recommendations made to the government by the Canadian Congress of Labour in this matter a few weeks ago. On page 1 of their memorandum to the government the congress says:
The congress urges the government to press for a firm international agreement on the abolition of all stocks of atomic and hydrogen weapons and the prohibition of the manufacture and use of such weapons, under effective international control. As a first step towards these ends the government should take the initiative to obtain an agreement to stop nuclear weapon tests.
Just what is to be gained, Mr. Speaker, by continuing to build still more powerful nuclear weapons? Apparently, both east and west now have a sufficient number of these weapons to destroy each other in a matter of hours, if not in a matter of minutes. What is to be gained by building still more? Surely, since no one nation can keep such tests a secret from other nations and since science cannot yet tell us just what the disastrous effects of these tests may be upon unborn generations, as human beings, whether Russian, American, British or Canadian, we are intelligent enough to reach some agreement to stop further tests as a first step in an agreement for effective international supervision of a disarmament program.
Lord Beaverbrook's powerful newspaper, the Daily Express, in its New Year's message to the British people on January 2, asked these questions:
What should be foremost in the minds of the people as the New Year opens? What should be their guiding light in the months that lie ahead?
The Daily Express gives these three answers:
(1)	War should be repudiated. It should be utterly dismissed from the thoughts of the public.
(2)	Armaments should be reduced to the utmost extent.
(3)	Above all, espouse the cause of world-wide control of atomic weapons. Press for it.
Urge it upon the leaders of the nations.
Atomic weapons have a particular horror for humanity. They hold a unique menace.
Nothing would contribute so much to easing the tensions that exist today as the knowledge that these terrible instruments of destruction had been immobilised.
Nothing could do more to relieve the world of its load of poison.
As the Canadian Congress of Labour points out, defence against communism is "not simply a matter of guns and planes and bombs, of armies and navies and air forces"; it is also a matter, to use the words of the congress, "of rooting out poverty and exploitation" wherever they exist. Only when
370	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy we can prove to the world that as a nation we are employing our national wealth and our national resources to root out poverty and exploitation at home, and particularly in those underdeveloped countries of the world, shall we be able to demonstrate to these people that democracy can give them more tangible benefits than can communism.
We welcome the government's proposal to increase its contribution under the Colombo plan. In the opinion of many of us that contribution is still too small. There are, moreover, a number of sectors of our domestic economy where poverty and exploitation still exist. The old age pensioner, for instance, who has to live on his $40 each month, judged by present-day living standards, is not very far removed from poverty. The employable unemployed who has exhausted his unemployment insurance and is forced to fall back upon municipal relief is oftentimes on the very edge of poverty. It is no credit to democracy, no credit to our federal government or to our provincial governments that we have another winter upon us and still no satisfactory agreement has been reached regarding the responsibility for those who are unfortunate enough to be unemployed employables.

There are many municipalities in Canada, Mr. Speaker, which are today without financial resources to meet their responsibility for social services and education; yet while we pride ourselves on our democratic freedoms and the strength of our free institutions, we permit petty jealousies as between governments at different levels to undermine the strength of those institutions, to undermine democracy itself at a time when democracy, as we know it, is engaged in a life and death struggle for existence against communism.
Here is another example, Mr. Speaker. Our sightless citizens whom we still subject to a means test, and to whom our government refuses to grant a small special allowance to cover the cost of guiding and other essential expenses, are oftentimes brought very close to poverty. Can Canada, with its vast national product, not spare just a few dollars for those sightless persons in the name and in the interests of democracy?
We were told in yesterday's press that in the last ten weeks 180 Canadian lives had been lost through fires. Tests show that in the great majority of cases inferior building


material and substandard houses have been the causes of those fires, and the cause of this appalling loss of life. Notwithstanding the improvements we have made in the National Housing Act, notwithstanding the increase in building that has come about, we have not yet seriously tackled the problem of providing houses in Canada for those who need them most. The majority of the houses built under the National Housing Act are sold to those who are in the $5,000 income bracket or higher. There are still no houses being built or made available that can be sold or rented at prices that tens of thousands of Canadians in the lower income brackets, Canadian couples wtih young families to support, can afford. Our major problem in housing is still with us. It is that of providing houses for those people.
While I am on this subject, I wonder whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare will take an opportunity soon to tell us whether or not his department considers taking some action in this field. In my opinion his department is in a better position than any other organization in this country to carry on a national, all-out educational campaign to show our people both how to prevent those fires and what to do when they occur. A very prominent specialist, a man who is employed by the insurance companies as a specialist in this field, Mr. Douglas Abbey- I think he is the standards engineer of the fire protection division of the underwriters laboratories of Canada-tells us that:
-an informed public would go a long way toward lowering the annual toll of lives lost in house fires.
What an opportunity there is for the Department of National Health and Welfare, which every month is in correspondence with the mothers of the children of our nation, to provide the homes with some form of guidance and instruction in this field. Of course the minister will run foul of provincial regulations and responsibilities. He may even find that his terms of reference and his budget will not permit him to take action along this line. If I know the Minister of National Health and Welfare, he is a man of vision, a humanitarian, and I am sure he is man enough to rise above those petty difficulties and do something for the children to whom his department is sending family allowance cheques every month.
The leader of the official opposition has already in this debate called attention to the need for the revision of some of our labour legislation. The grievances of a large group of railway employees still remain unsolved, and no edict of the Prime Minister that these men should not go on strike is a solution of

that problem. Railways are essential in this country, and if because of competition they must be operated at a loss, then the employees of the railways should not be called upon to bear the brunt of those losses. Some means must be found other than the undemocratic method of depriving these men of a right that has been long established as a part of our collective bargaining system.
Much has been said already about unemployment insurance. I realize that the Department of Labour is watching this act very closely, and that the legislation requires continual revision to meet the needs of the day. There is one phase of this act to which I should like to direct the attention of the house.
I am given to understand that an employee who has suffered an industrial accident for which he is paid workmen's compensation suffers some loss in his unemployment insurance. While he is receiving compensation no payments are made on his behalf into the unemployment insurance fund. If after returning to work he finds himself unemployed, the number of days to which he would normally be entitled are reduced by reason of the fact that he has been drawing workmen's compensation.
It does not seem fair to me that a workman who has suffered an industrial accident, probably through no fault of his own, and who is placed on workmen's compensation of say 75 per cent of his wages for a period of time, should be penalized further by having his entitlement to unemployment insurance reduced by reason of that fact. I would suggest to the minister that some study be given to this problem and means found whereby workers who are injured and in receipt of workmen's compensation shall not have to suffer later on because of that fact.
I understand that hon. members generally are attempting to co-operate in keeping their speeches down to 25 or 30 minutes, and as a matter of fact I have been warned by our whip that if I exceed the 30-minute limit I am not likely to get on again in a hurry. So I had better watch my time.
There is just one further matter I should like to mention. I was disappointed personally, and I am sure many others are also disappointed, that no mention was made in the speech from the throne of the setting up of a Canada council to support the arts in Canada. It is now about five years since the famous Massey commission recommended the setting up of such a council, but when we heard the statement the other day by the Prime Minister that the government does not contemplate setting up such a council this year we were further disappointed.
The Address-Mr. Thatcher
It is difficult to understand why a prime minister who sets such a high value on culture as does our Prime Minister should take an attitude like this on this matter. The Prime Minister is a man of culture, he appreciates culture and he comes from a province where recently a Gallup poll showed there were more people supporting the idea of government subsidies for the arts than in any other province of Canada. He comes from a province where artistic culture is probably better established than anywhere else in Canada.
We wonder just what it is the Prime Minister and his cabinet are afraid of, for they must be afraid of something when five years are allowed to go by since that famous report was made. I merely want to say in closing that I trust the Prime Minister and those in his cabinet who are interested in Canadian culture will review the situation, and that before this session ends we shall have a recommendation for the setting up of this long-promised council.
Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake
Centre): Mr. Speaker, my first remarks this session must be directed to the Minister of Finance. In his budget speech last year the minister stated that in 1955 Canada would probably have a gross national product of $25-25 billion. On the basis of that gross national product he intimated that the federal government would probably have a deficit of $160 million. Fortunately for the people of Canada, the minister was apparently somewhat conservative, because instead of a gross national product of $25-25 billion for last year the figure was $26-4 billion, or $1-2 billion more than expected. I would remind the house at this time of what the minister said in his budget speech last year, at page 2733 of Hansard:
I propose, therefore, to recommend a tax structure which, as closely as I can estimate, would produce a balanced budget if we had a gross national product of about $26 billion.
In view of the fact that the gross national product was $26 [DOT] 4 billion I think it is reasonable to expect that the government will come reasonably close to balancing its budget.
I was interested to note that in a year-end statement, the Minister of Trade and Commerce made the prophecy that in the coming year our gross national product was going to reach $28 billion. If that should happen it is quite likely that in the coming year the government will have a fairly substantial surplus.
I should like to express the hope at this time that the government will use that surplus to give our people a substantial tax cut.

The Address-Mr. Thatcher I think tax cuts are needed tor very obvious reasons. In the first place, they are needed to bring relief to those in the lower income groups. In the second place they are needed to spur investment in Canadian mines, industry and business.
If the minister should find it possible to bring about tax reduction within the confines of a balanced budget, I would hope that the reduction will be in the field of personal income tax. I would hope it may be possible to increase the income tax exemption for married people from $2,000 to $3,000 and for single people from $1,000 to $1,800. I believe such action would be most beneficial. I sincerely hope that the government will not wait for an election year before they grant such tax reduction.
A good deal has been said already in this debate about the wheat crisis in western Canada, and I should like to refer to it briefly. It has been pointed out many times that the wheat surplus in the west recently reached an historic peak of almost one billion bushels. Out west we have grain in our barns, in our stables, in our granaries, in our elevators. Indeed, many farmers have grain out in their fields which they have not been able to get in.
As a result the great majority of farmers have been unable to deliver enough wheat to pay their ordinary living expenses. During the past four years farm income on the prairies has dropped by almost two-thirds. I do not think it is necessary for me to belabour the point to this house that the western farmer is in real difficulty. The important question we must face this session is, what can be done about it? Is there any practical solution? Dozens of proposals have already been made in this debate. Dozens of other proposals have been made outside the house, throughout the west. Some of those proposals are reasonable; some of them contain food for thought but many of them, in my opinion, have been little more than economic nonsense.
As I see it, this issue is not a political one. It is far too important. I think all political parties should get together to see if they cannot find a practical solution to this problem. In the west, in the past few months, I have asked dozens of farmers this question:	If
you were the Prime Minister of Canada, what would you do to solve the wheat crisis? Most of them would look at me for a moment, smile a little, and then quite frankly admit that they did not know precisely what an over-all solution would be.
The fact is that, as I see it, there is no easy answer. There is no pat solution. There is no magic formula. If there had been, I am

quite sure the government would have been intelligent enough to find it many months ago. What are some of the solutions that have been seriously suggested in this house and elsewhere? I should like to comment on five or six of them.
Some people say that we should give away our wheat to the countries of Asia, or possibly of Europe, as a solution. Speaking for the C.C.F. group the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), as shown on page 88 of Hansard, took such an attitude. Personally I feel that Canada should not hesitate to make modest gifts to needy countries for humanitarian reasons if there is a famine or something of that nature. But to propose that a billion dollars should be set aside for such a purpose is, in my opinion, neither responsible nor practical.

It has been suggested that we should take sterling from the United Kingdom in payment for wheat. That suggestion has been mooted a great deal in western Canada. I do not believe that is much more practical at this time than the first suggestion. As has been mentioned in this house already, Mr. Gordon Bowen, the United Kingdom senior trade commissioner, came out to Saskatoon a short time before Christmas to address a farm union meeting and was

asked this question from the floor by a farmer:	"How much more wheat would
Canada sell to Britain if we were prepared to take sterling in payment?" Mr. Bowen made the flat and categorical answer: "You would not sell one solitary extra bushel more." So that disposes of this solution.
A third suggestion which is frequently made is that we should cut the price of wheat to encourage consumption. I certainly believe that the Canadian wheat board at all times must meet price competition, because if it does not it is going to lose its traditional markets. But my understanding is that it is already doing this. Today prices paid to United States, United Kingdom, German, Belgian and Argentine producers, and to producers in other countries, are considerably higher than the Canadian export price.
From past experience it seems very doubtful that a cut in price would sell more Canadian wheat. In the depression years the price went as low as 30 cents a bushel, and we did not sell very much more. In fact in some cases we actually sold less, because some of the countries put up the tariff to protect their own home producers against cheap Canadian wheat. It seems to me that if Canada cut her wheat prices today, probably Australia, Argentina and the United States would soon follow suit. None of us would sell any more wheat. Canada probably would not regain a larger proportion of the market, and in the long run the western farmers would be in a worse predicament than when we started. So I reject this third suggestion as not being feasible.
A fourth solution which has sometimes been suggested is that we should reduce the amount of acreage sown to wheat. If, to the extent that wheat acreage is taken out of production, rye, oats, barley, corn or hay is planted in its place, I am all for it. But I think it is contrary to economic sense and to humanitarian principles to encourage a farmer to take his land out of production altogether, when there are so many hungry people in the world.
A fifth suggestion, of which we have heard a good deal in this house, is that we should accept barter in return for our wheat. Personally I have nothing against barter. As a matter of fact, if a nation could be found which had something that Canada could use, to barter for wheat, I would be in favour of it. However, I have not been able to learn of any such country. I would very respectfully point out that those who suggest barter as a method of getting rid of wheat should be more specific. They should talk less in generalities and tell us precisely what country wants to barter with Canada
The Address-Mr. Thatcher for wheat. Then, if it is practical, let us go ahead with it. Personally I am rather of the opinion that barter would have as much effect on our wheat surplus as a pail of water taken from the Ottawa river would have in lowering its level.
A sixth proposal sometimes put forward is that we should scrap the Canadian wheat board and get back to the Winnipeg grain exchange. This school of thought proposes that we should let the law of supply and demand set the price of wheat. Personally I would hope that this course is not followed, because if the law of supply and demand were setting the price of wheat today, with our huge supplies on hand, the price would soon drop very sharply and drastically.
I could go on about some of the other proposals which have been made in this house to get rid of our wheat surplus. As I see it, none of them would do very much more than nibble at the crux of the problem. In my opinion it is a mistake for any citizen to feel that the government, by waving a magic wand of some kind, can get rid of this wheat. Unfortunately our grain economy is not under the control of the government; it is under the control of an uncontrollable world market.
I have always felt, and I feel more strongly than ever today, that the most practical way for the prairie farmers to get rid of large quantities of this grain is to feed it to livestock and poultry. I believe that such a program should channel some of our borderline grades of feed wheat into livestock consumption rather than into human consumption. I certainly do not suggest that this is the over-all answer. It is not, but it would put a good deal of cash into the hands of the farmer.
Some people will immediately say this is no solution because as soon as you feed grain to livestock and hogs you will have a glut of those particular farm products. I admit there is that danger, but apparently we are not very close to it at the moment. Today we are consuming practically all the beef and hogs we produce in this country. As a matter of fact, lately we have been even consuming a little of the United States production, because since November 12 last, carload after carload of steers has been coming into the Toronto market. Since that date approximately 5,400 United States cattle have been imported for slaughter by Canadian packing houses.
I say that through immigration, through natural increase, our population is growing by 400,000 per year. That is a pretty healthy increase but I do not think it is enough. If the government really wants to do something

The Address-Mr. Thatcher
about the wheat crisis it should increase immigration. It should bring in not 125,000 people a year but 250,000, so that our home markets will be enlarged by people who will eat meat and dairy products. That will be a secure market. That would be the place for our farmers to start to get rid of some of their grain. Our farmers could then safely diversify. They could feed a lot of this wheat to cattle. If the glut is to be ended the government must build up our home market.
I would also remind the house that there is yet another market for Canadian meat products. Today, for reasons of price, Canada is not taking advantage of the provisions of the Geneva trade agreement which permit us to ship large quantities of meat to the United States. For example, as far as cattle are concerned there is a tariff today of 1J cents per pound on the first 200,000 calves shipped to the United States, and a similar tariff on the first 400,000 cattle over 700 pounds shipped to that country. In the first 11 months of 1955 we only shipped 4,600 calves and 55,000 cattle south of the border. This means in effect that we only took advantage of 1-6 per cent of our minimum market for calves in the United States and 14 per cent of our minimum market for cattle.
What about hogs? Under the Geneva trade agreement we are permitted to send unlimited quantities of hogs to the United States by paying a tariff of 1 cent per pound. Yet last year, again for reasons of price, we only shipped 8,212 hogs. As far as sheep are concerned, we can sell unlimited quantities by paying a tariff of $3 a head, but in the 11-month period we only exported 8,382 sheep. Much the same situation exists in connection with poultry.
I say we are missing the boat. I admit that the United States already has large surpluses of certain meat products. Nevertheless they signed a trade agreement with us which permits Canadian livestock to enter their market when the price is sufficiently attractive. If they live up to the agreement I see no reason why Canadian farmers cannot compete over the ensuing years with a reasonable degree of success.
I repeat that, as I see it, the most practical way for parliament to fight the grain crisis is to encourage our prairie farmers to diversify their economy. If diversification is to be successful our home market must be built up, and the United States market must be cultivated. Personally I think the legislation announced by the government in the speech from the throne, which has as its purpose the paying of abnormal storage charges on wheat, will be welcomed in western Canada by pretty 
nearly everyone. At the same time I think the government erred in making loans available through the banks instead of making advances on farm-stored grain. However, I am going to comment on that legislation at the appropriate time.
I said a moment ago that in my opinion it is not reasonable to expect the government to solve the wheat crisis by waving a magic wand. However, there is one place where I think the government can be severely criticized. As has already been pointed out by various speakers, there are large quantities of elevator space available in western Canada. Some people suggest that there is space for 100 million bushels. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said this morning that it was only about 58 million. Whether the figure is 100 million or 58 million, that space should be filled. I think the situation which permits such empty elevator space to exist is inexcusable. The minister or the responsible authorities should tell the railroads that they are expected to give top priority to box cars for moving grain. If such action were taken I think it would do more than any other single thing to alleviate immediately the cash picture in the west.

Mr. Speaker, in the more leisurely days of the past it has been customary for all hon. members taking part in the throne speech debate to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As far as I can determine it has been customary to carry out this bit of good manners even on occasions when the recipients were not particularly deserving because their efforts were only fair. However, those leisurely days are gone forever, and we now find ourselves operating on a schedule. We are faced with the problem of conducting ourselves suitably in this new age of efficiency and expedition.
We find ourselves in circumstances where debates, arguments and controversies must be carried on under a pre-set schedule. It is not surprising, therefore, that many hon. members rising to take part in this debate this year find themselves torn between two desires. On the one hand, they wish to comply with the spirit of the new rules and get down to the business at hand as quickly as possible. On the other hand, they do not wish to break away from the traditions of gallantry and good manners evidenced by complimenting the mover and seconder. Our desires in that respect are even less

compatible this year because not only gallantry but chivalry are involved on this occasion, since for the first time in the history of this parliament the mover of the address has been a lady.
So here we are impaled on the horns of a dilemma. Shall we proceed to the business before us immediately we rise to speak and run the risk of appearing rude, or shall we carry on the traditional courtesies to which we have become so accustomed and run the danger of infringing on the time of some other hon. member who may have something really worth while to contribute to the debate? By way of compromise I should like on this occasion, not only on behalf of myself but, if they will permit me, on behalf of all hon. members planning to take part in the debate, to congratulate most heartily the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I turn now to the speech from the throne itself, and I wish to quote one short excerpt. It reads:
Canada has enjoyed, on the whole, a high level of prosperity. Some sectors of the economy have not fully participated in this increased well-being.
Then it goes on to make reference to wheat. I presume, therefore, that one of the sectors which is not participating fully is the industry of agriculture. If the statement refers to agriculture, it is an understatement almost without parallel. I say that for the reason that agriculture is a keystone of our whole economy. I think it is fair to say that about 50 per cent of the people in Canada either directly or indirectly depend upon agriculture for their livelihood. Agriculture is therefore a vital part of our economy. Merely to say in passing that it is a sector which is not sharing fully in the general high prosperity is somewhat similar to a medical doctor's saying, when reporting on the health of a patient, that the patient looked fit all over with one minor exception, namely that his throat was slit from ear to ear.
We should remember that every depression in Canada since confederation began in the first instance because the farmers in this country did not have the purchasing power with which they could go to town and buy a lantern, a set of harness, a tractor or a light plant, as the case may be.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has taken exception to the fact that some hon. members have seen fit to criticize the fact that our agricultural surpluses are accumulating, especially in wheat. He took the attitude that surpluses are an unmixed blessing, and that we do not ever want to be in the position of old Mother Hubbard. That is
The Address-Mr. MacLean perfectly true. But we should remember that almost anything, if carried to excess, can cease to be an advantage. If out of her abundance nature showers us with material blessings in the way of food, raw materials for clothing and so on, and if this country of ours becomes, literally and figuratively, a land overflowing with milk and honey, it is a good thing provided that special difficulties are not created. In most cases special difficulties of economics arise under those circumstances. It should be remembered that the promised land which overflowed with milk and honey is now a desert. Anything can become excessive. It is always possible to reach the point where virtues become vices and where assets become liabilities. When the minister put his defence of surpluses on those grounds I could not help being reminded of a young lady in my province who went to a psychiatrist complaining bitterly that her husband claimed that she was crazy simply because she liked pancakes. The psychiatrist said, "Your husband must be a most unreasonable man, because I myself like pancakes". She said, "Is that really so? You must come over to my house some time and look at mine. I have a whole trunkful".
Surpluses in themselves are not something of which we should be afraid. But if agricultural surpluses mean that we are going to have a depression in agriculture, with the attendant dislocation of our whole economy, we must be concerned with excess surpluses. If this government are developing a guilt complex over the present state of affairs as did Macbeth after he committed his well-known crime, I suppose they will have misgivings about their course of action. As you will remember, Mr. Speaker, under those circumstances Macbeth was visited by several characters from the hereafter. I do not think it has been definitely established whether or not that sort of thing ever occurs with the cabinet but if it does it might be appropriate that one of the visitors the cabinet might have from the hereafter would be one of the same visitors that Macbeth had on that memorable night. Among the ghosts who visited him was a farmer who had hanged himself on thinking of the prospects of a bounteous harvest. That is about the position in which the farmers of Canada find themselves at the present time.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the situation in agriculture-at least in my part of the country; I do not pretend to be able to speak for the west-is extremely serious. Agriculture cannot continue to exist in the economic atmosphere in which it now finds itself. It is true that the result will not be felt for some time. It is true that the farmers are still carrying on trying to make ends
376	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. MacLean meet while their machinery is wearing out, their soil is being mined and they are drawing on their capital in every way. It is also true, especially in my province, that farms are still being operated by elderly people who cannot, at their stage in life, change to some other more profitable occupation. Hence they decide to mine their soil, let their plant run down and eke out a living in that fashion until they are old enough to qualify for admittance to an old people's home. The tragedy of it is that among the rising generation there is almost no one to whom agriculture appeals sufficiently, on economic grounds, to entice him to the land to carry on where his father left off.
Defenders of the present agricultural situation may take refuge in statistics to prove that farmers are not as badly off as we farmers think we are. I should like to point out that statistics are a good thing if properly interpreted and if used for the purpose for which they were intended, but one should not forget that there are a great many things that statistics do not tell. When statistics say that the net farm income of the Canadian farmer has dropped by a certain percentage, it means more than just a few cold figures. It means that with every percentage drop in the net income there are hundreds if not thousands of farms in Canada that have been operating for a century which must go out of business. These farms rapidly reach the point where they have little or no market value as agricultural land, quickly reach the point of no return, and are thus permanently lost to the Canadian people as a potential source of food and clothing.
It may be true that a few favoured farmers are still doing reasonably well. There may be farmers who find themselves with a large plant, a local market, good land and other special circumstances which put them in a favoured position. But all the farmers in Canada are not large producers. I do not have the figures for Canada, but it is a fact that in the United States 50 per cent of the agricultural production is produced by 10 per cent of the farmers. The other 90 per cent are important people, too. If they are eliminated from our economy, dire results will ensue. So I hope no one will try to dismiss the very difficult situation in which thousands of Canadian farmers find themselves by saying that farm net income has only dropped by a certain percentage in the last year.
As I said before, statistics can be deceiving. It is said that at one time there was a lumber camp in New Brunswick in which there were 100 men and two female cooks employed. Some statistician reporting on the state of the


camp, and noting that one of the men had married one of the cooks, reported that 1 per cent of the men had married 50 per cent of the women.
There are three possible explanations of the government's apparent lack of concern about present conditions. One possible explanation is that the government do not realize the seriousness of the situation. It may be, too, that they know what is happening but think it is a good thing and are willing to let it happen. They may argue that our economy is out of balance, that we produce too much food, that there are too many farmers and some of them must be eliminated by the cold laws of economics. It may be that they realize the situation but find themselves powerless to do anything effective about it.
But agriculture is of tremendous importance to the Canadian people. It is, I believe, of vital importance not only for economic reasons but for other reasons as well. Some of the most obvious economic reasons, of course, are that we in Canada are one of the best fed nations in the world. This results from the efficiency of Canadian agriculture. If Canadian agriculture is permanently damaged, that will not continue to be the case. We depend on agriculture for many other raw materials besides food. We depend on agriculture for much of our clothing, and in a broader sense we depend on the soil for the raw materials of the pulp and paper industry and many other things. About 50 per cent of the Canadian people are dependent, directly or indirectly, on the products of the soil for their livelihood.
In this connection I should like to quote briefly from a small pamphlet entitled, "At the first table". It is written by Mr. Stewart Page, the agricultural representative for North Simcoe. He says:
More and more we are learning to look at the land as the major source of real wealth, and to farming as a high art. We are learning that while soil fertility is highly perishable, it is also a renewable resource, and herein lies the art of good farming-How to extract a living from the soil in such a manner as to be able to pass on the farm to the next generation in a more fertile condition than we found it?
What we need most for Canada, and for Simcoe county, is a readjustment of basic values so that the dollar will once more be the servant of man, not its master. Half of the world is hungry and needs our surplus food but we have priced ourselves out of the world market. Over half of our soils are hungry but we have put such a high value on the services of labour, industry and commerce that there is seldom enough left over to feed the soil.
The crux of the whole problem today is that our greatest natural resource, the soil, must subsist as best it can on the scraps left over from the banquets of our highly artificial way of life. This

was the way of all vanished civilizations of the past and we are travelling along the same road but at the speed of jet propulsion.
There is a very good sociological reason, too, why the economy of our rural areas and small towns must be preserved. After all, it still is a fact that the rural areas and the small towns are the wellsprings from which our civilization draws its leaders for the most part. In that connection I should like to quote very briefly from the footnote in a book recently written by Louis Bromfield entitled "From my Experience". This footnote appears on page 53:
It is not perhaps without significance that the vast majority of the names listed in Who's Who are those of men who came from farms or from small communities in agricultural territory. Even with the immense development of industry and cities, the leadership of the country in all fields seems still to come very largely from rural areas where a sense of responsibility and maturity grows from work and contacts with the soil and with livestock, and where, more often than not, a boy or a girl learns to work and to think for what he gets in this life.
From the point of view of public health it is important, too. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) pointed out very forcibly the other day figures which are shocking so far as the physical condition of the average Canadian youth is concerned. I believe I am right in saying that this condition is worse in the large metropolitan areas. As the agricultural industry is starved, more and more people are forced to move into metropolitan areas and more and more people find themselves growing up in the larger cities where life itself is perverted. The justification for the existence of many of these cities no longer exists in this day of rapid transportation, instantaneous communication and the atom bomb.
The hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Reinke) pointed out recently one of the symptoms of the unnatural life lived by thousands of people in large cities. He pointed out that conditions were such that children on many streets in some of our cities are no safer than they would be in the jungles of Africa.
The obvious question to ask is, what is the answer? One of the most thorny problems facing all Canadians at the present time, of course, is the question of our wheat surplus, but I do not intend to take up the time of the house on that matter. However, in some other agricultural fields we do not have a surplus, yet the situation is little better.
I come from an area where the chief cash crop is potatoes. At the present time the farmers are asked to operate and to continue to produce one of the most basic foods of our country at a continual loss, and this at a time when Canada has not a net surplus of
The Address-Mr. MacLean potatoes. Those producers of potatoes are asked to sell their product on an unprotected market, subject to being flooded with surplus potatoes from' the United States with no duty chargeable on them. Those same farmers are asked to buy much of their equipment on the protected markets of the industrial areas of central Canada. We in the maritimes feel that this is not a reasonable or a fair state of affairs, and we hope that action will be taken to rectify it.
Some people will say that it is easy to talk, but what are we to do? If we go to the United States and point out these inequalities in our tariffs as between the two countries, they will say they must not be offended because they will retaliate with some other tariff. I feel very strongly that the United States people are reasonable, and if the situation were fairly explained, not so much to the experts but to the legislators of the United States who are required to make a decision, a reasonable decision could be arrived at.
A few weeks ago another member of this house and I had the privilege, along with a number of members of parliament from various European countries, of being guests of the United States government for some time in that country. While in Washington I found myself seated at dinner next to a very well-known United States representative. He asked me about the state of the economy in the maritime provinces. Among other things I mentioned this matter of the depressed state of the potato industry, which concerns us in many areas there. In passing I mentioned the tariff situation with which we are expected to cope. I said that our growers were not very happy about having to sell their product in the United States over a tariff of 351 cents a hundredweight while United States potatoes come into their market duty free.
His reaction was, "I could not agree with them more. I think it is an unreasonable state of affairs." If he were a typical United States citizen described by the defenders of the present situation, I would have expected him to say, "It serves them right, because if we do anything for the potato grower, we shall have to do something for the apple grower, too."
We in the maritimes have the growing feeling that the horizons of almost all federal governments are limited to a varying extent. We have the feeling that the horizons of most federal governments are bound on the east by the St. Lawrence valley and on the west by the great lakes. We feel strongly that it is not only the members of the governments themselves who err in this direction, but the whole of parliament. None of

The Address-Mr. MacLean us is as well acquainted with our country as we should be. As a suggestion toward correcting this situation, I would like to see members of parliament given the right to travel free at least twice a year on the air lines of our country so that members whose homes are in the extremities could have the opportunity to visit their constituencies, and those from central Canada could avail themselves of the opportunity to become personally acquainted with the problems that exist in other parts of Canada.
In the maritimes we have the feeling that if a problem of national importance arises, either in our part of the country or in the west, it is just simply beyond the ken of the government. We are not pleased with the lethargy of this government with regard to the problems facing the agricultural industry of this country and the west and the maritimes in general. Apologists for the government will say, "After all, you cannot expect a cure overnight. This is a democracy, and a democracy is like a good wife, very attractive but not fast." That is their excuse for not doing anything about it. I would point out that this is not a legitimate excuse for not doing anything. Action must be taken immediately to correct the situation if irreparable damage is not to be caused.
In the maritimes we have the feeling that the lethargy of the government is proportional, perhaps, to the square, or even the cube, of the distance of the problem away from Ottawa, and we are getting absolutely fed up with this state of affairs. Therefore we have two major problems facing the Canadian people at the present time. On the one hand, generally speaking, we have the depressed state of the agricultural industry, and on the other hand the fact that the maritime provinces, and to a lesser extent the west, continues in a state of chronic depression.
When my ancestors, and the ancestors of all the people of the maritimes, were pushed, either by religious persecution or by economic pressures, from the countries of Europe, they came to what are now the maritime provinces because they looked like a land of promise, and they were a land of promise. They progressed and prospered wondrously well for many years, as a matter of fact, until confederation. For more than 80 years confederation has hung like a killing blight over the economy of the maritimes. That is a tragic thing to have to say; nevertheless it is so. We in the maritimes whose ancestors came to a land of plenty find ourselves forced to migrate again because of economic conditions. Our patience is running out.
[Mi MacLean.]

The patience of the agricultural people of Canada is running out. After all, this government is now starting on its twenty-first year in office, and the problems of the maritimes and of agriculture remain unsolved. The farmers of Canada and the people of the maritimes are dissatisfied with this situation, because they remember that even Rip Van Winkle woke up after 20 years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted at the outset of my remarks to pay my respects to the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and the seconder (Mr. Lafiamme) of the motion now before the house. I think this is probably one of the finer practices which have grown up over the years concerning this debate. The mover and seconder are placed at a disadvantage in that they are the first to speak in the debate. They are notified in advance, and this year they certainly appear to have done considerable work, from the efforts they have made.
I am not so well acquainted with the seconder of the address, as he has just come to the house; but judging from the way he conducted himself I would say that it augurs well for the people of Canada when we have men of such ability standing for public office. It augurs well for the people of his own constituency and province.
I should like to say something about the mover of the address. She has handled herself with obvious distinction and ability while in this chamber, and I would say has been far above the average in her attendance and conduct of affairs. In particular I should like to refer to her work as a committee member, for it is in committee that the ability of a member is made known. I noted in the committees in which I have been associated with the hon. member that she has been most faithful in attendance and has shown a distinct ability in the conduct of the affairs of the committee. If necessary she can be very forceful.
If I were in authority I would recommend to the Prime Minister that when he is looking for a way in which to express the wishes of the government by giving advancement to hon. members, he would be well advised to look with favour upon the mover of this address, not because she is a woman but because of the ability which she undoubtedly has and which she has manifested in this chamber.
I should like to refer now to a matter which has to do with money. Loans of up to $500 are controlled by the Small Loans Act of 1939. I have no complaint whatsoever with regard to the majority of moneylenders who operate under this act. I am fully aware of the great need for such a service, because obviously

the banking system under which we operate has not met the needs and wishes of a certain cross section of our population. I am aware also of the great good which moneylenders have accomplished, especially during and following world war II when many of our people had need of immediate cash for emergency purposes and to consolidate obligations incurred while in the armed forces or during the course of the war. This money was not available from any other source.
There has sprung up in the business sections of most of our communities numerous loan companies and moneylenders which are doing a most aggressive business in lending money, not solely to meet the necessities of persons but to satisfy the desires and whims of the Canadian people. Our newspapers contain large advertisements urging people to borrow money and using such slogans as "I like to lend money" or "We have the money you need in the amount you want" or "Phone for your loan in one trip". Many other catch phrases are used.
The slogans I have given were taken from the daily newspapers, but our motor buses and street cars blare forth the need to hurry to such and such a loan company to borrow up to $2,400 without any guarantee being required. Billboards impress upon the passing motorist how simple it is to get money without any security. The radio and television impress the listener and viewer with the simplicity of getting money for a trip to Florida or the purchase of a new television set. Many of the companies operating in Canada do so with United States capital, and naturally the profits of their operations go to United States investors.
We seem to have forgotten the fatherly and wise financial advice given by our bankers. It may be that our bankers have expressed too much concern, or shown too much restraint in the manner in which they make advances'. We forget also that we have the privilege of banding together in credit unions which are growing in numbers so rapidly throughout this country. Money can be borrowed from a credit union at a rate usually not exceeding 1 per cent, after investigation by the other members of the credit union.
Under the provisions of the Small Loans Act a moneylender may charge 2 per cent per month for a period of 15 months and 1 per cent per month thereafter on loans of not more than $500. On this basis, in the year 1940-that is 15 years ago-the Canadian people borrowed approximately $20 million from loan companies and moneylenders. As I say, these were in amounts not exceeding $500. By January 1, 1954, the amount borrowed by the Canadian people during the
The Address-Mr. D. F. Brown preceding year had grown to $175 million. Owing to the power of publicity and advertising, it is estimated that in the calendar year 1955 the Canadian people borrowed approximately $200 million in amounts under $500.
Even with this class of loan, if it were divided among all the Canadian population of 16 million it would mean that each man, woman and child in Canada had borrowed approximately $14. However, this is not exactly the true picture, since it covers only loans up to an amount of $500. I have been told by the manager of a reputable loan company that the average loan today is for an amount far in excess of $500.
I hold in my hand a report from a commercial agency in my constituency showing the chattel mortgages that were filed in the county clerk's office in one week; this happens to be the week of November 30, 1955. This indicates that altogether there were 115 loans of which registration was made, and of those 115 loans there were only 18 under $500. Those over $2,000 numbered 5. As 5 and 18 make 23, you will readily see that 92 of these loans were for amounts between $500 and $2,000, in other words, approximately 90 per cent of the loans made.
I hold in my hand also a further report, for the week of December 14, 1955, which shows a similar situation. In that week there were 141 loans, of which 16 were under $500. Five were over $2,000, leaving 120 between $500 and $2,000. This leaves about the same percentage referred to above. This indicates to me that between the amounts of $500 and $2,000 there is a vast field of borrowing, a great deal of which is without proper departmental control or supervision.
We may reasonably ask why we should concern ourselves with any supervision in this field. After all, this is a free country, and business should not be interfered with by a paternal government. My answer to this would be that, if two and two are four, it is reasonable to assume that 200 and 200 would then be 400. If $500 in 1939 was of value-and it was-to the extent of $500 at that time, all will agree that today it is the equivalent of about $1,000 to $1,500 or in that neighbourhood. Therefore if it was necessary and beneficial to the Canadian people in 1939, it is equally of benefit to us in 1956 to have an increased amount of control over the loans made under this act, especially since the economy has been expanding so rapidly.
From the investigations I have made I find that in connection with loans up to $500 there are very few infractions of the act or of ethics in the operation of the act, but it is between the sums of $500 and $2,000
380	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. D. F. Brown that there is no control, and I regret to say that in many respects the ethical standards of the moneylenders in many cases leave something to be desired. Let me repeat that I have no quarrel with borrowing for needs such as medical and hospitalization necessities or any other necessities for the home or the family, but I do not believe that we should instil in our people the belief that money can be gained easier by the toss of the pen than by the tug of the plow.
Most of this borrowing is secured by an assignment of wages given by the borrower and directed to the employer, or by obtaining security on the individual's household furniture, motor car or other chattel he might happen to have. When default is made, the more reliable companies interview the borrower to see wherein the difficulty lies, to find out why he has made default and try to help him to correct the practice into which he has fallen. They will try to work out a solution that will be of benefit both to the borrower and to the moneylender. But the more unscrupulous moneylender will seize or threaten to seize the goods and chattels pledged, and some may take garnishee proceedings on the wages, or threaten or cajole the borrower into refinancing the loan, for which an extra charge is made by the moneylender, and often a bonus is extracted.
It is in this particular case where, I believe, the greatest evil results; in the refinancing of these loans when the borrower falls into default. Legal expenses are added, though I have not been able to find out whether they are incurred. Insurance in large amounts is added. I have one example here in which insurance of $177 has been added on a loan of $950.
Over the years the government has done much to lessen the fears which beset our people. Family allowances have reduced the fear of youth; old age security has reduced the fear of old age; blind allowances have reduced the fear of blindness; unemployment insurance has reduced the fear of unemployment. Now I urge that controls be extended to reduce the fear of the loan shark.
Persons borrowing money are living in a state of acute fear, to such an extent that they will not give information with respect to their borrowings for fear of reprisals by the moneylenders.
However, I have in my hand evidence that excessive amounts are being charged on loans in excess of $500. I hold here a copy of an affidavit filed in the supreme court of Ontario in an action instituted by a moneylender. It is his own affidavit and in it he claims 33 per cent interest on the balance of principal which, in the schedule to the affidavit,
[Mr. Brown (Essex West).!

appears to be $1,270. At the rate of 33 per cent he is claiming some $590 per annum as interest. I will be pleased to turn this information over to the persons in authority when the time arrives.
I have also interviewed a borrower who obtained a loan of $800 and had to repay therefor the sum of $1,200 within a period of two years. This loan has been completely paid off. I have interviewed another borrower who obtained a loan of over $3,600 for which slightly over $4,400 had to be repaid. This loan was also repaid in full within the period of a year, but the rate of interest works out to about 30 per cent per annum.
All these claims for interest may be perfectly legal, but in my opinion they are highly excessive and should be controlled. I am therefore recommending that the provisions of the Small Loans Act be extended to control loans up to $2,000. Loans over $500, as I have pointed out, are where the great evil enters the picture. Up to $500 everything seems to be in order because such loans are quite closely controlled by the department of insurance.
Borrowers of amounts over $500 are often faced with the necessity of paying a bonus to obtain a loan. The borrower is in such a financial position that he wants to raise a sum of money; and for various reasons, usually because of his credit standing, the moneylender will require that he either pay a cash bonus, or he will give him a loan of a stated amount taking therefor a mortgage for a larger amount. Of course, in the first place a person of this type would probably be better off if he was not given a loan, because on the basis of his past record in handling money he is not in a position to handle it in such a way as to come out of the deal profitably.
If the terms of repayment are too onerous and the borrower makes default for one month the unscrupulous moneylender will, after the exercise of pressure, enter into a refinancing arrangement under which the first loan and bonus are absorbed in an arrangement whereby a second bonus is taken, until eventually the property of the borrower is so encumbered that any equity in the chattel or real estate disappears, and then possession is taken over by the moneylender.
This actually came to my attention recently in a case in my own constituency which is also on record in the supreme court of Ontario wherein, from correspondence with the moneylender's solicitor, I find that the borrower approached the finance company for a loan of $2,000, which he obtained. The security given was a mortgage for $2,500 with

interest being charged at 2 per cent per month on the $2,000. In other words the actual money advanced had interest added at 2 per cent per month. The mortgage was to run for a period of six months, when the whole amount was to become due and payable.
At the expiration of the six-month period the borrower was not in a position to pay the balance of the $2,500. So he approached the moneylender and an arrangement was entered into whereby a further bonus of $500 was added to the $2,500 and a rate of interest of 2 per cent per month on the whole $3,000 was inserted in the contract. Therefore the borrower wound up by getting $2,000 cash and giving security for $3,000, with interest at 2 per cent per month on the $3,000.
Eventually default was made on the mortgage and it was foreclosed. The property was lost and, incidentally, the borrower's family were separated, the wife going to one part of the country to find a job and the husband to another part of the country to find employment.
A further unsatisfactory practice which I believe is not prohibited by the act is where a loan is made for a stated amount and an amount equivalent to the first monthly payment is deducted immediately and interest charged on the whole loan. A case has come to my attention recently where the first monthly payment was deducted by the moneylender immediately the loan was given. The loan has not been repaid yet, and it will be interesting to find what adjustment is made by the moneylender when the loan is repaid in .full.
All such practices, which I am sure can be repeated and magnified many times by many members of the house, tend to stain the reputation of the legitimate and reputable loan companies and moneylenders who are trying to do a good job by maintaining high ethical standards and by retaining a reputation for fair dealing in the performance of a worthwhile service. I therefore suggest to the government that an examination be made into the whole practice of personal loans up to $5,000 to see what can be done to protect the citizens of our country, and to remove some of the unsatisfactory practices which now appear to be in vogue.
Here again I realize the difficulty in getting evidence of such malpractice because of the fear of people in coming forward to give evidence. First of all, they do not want other people to know about their financial dealings, their banking practices and their personal affairs. Second, they are afraid that if they do come forward to give evidence the loans which they at that time have will be jeopardized and they will suffer considerable loss.
The Address-Mr. D. F. Brown
I have received a number of anonymous letters telling of sordid cases, some in Montreal, others in Hull, Toronto and elsewhere, none of which letters can be used because they are anonymous. But I am sure these matters are within the knowledge of the industry itself, and I am glad to see that the Canadian consumer loan association is most anxious that any unsavoury practice be stamped out. As a matter of fact I have a letter from the president of the association, which states in part:
The Canadian consumer loan association wholeheartedly supports your view that legislation should be drawn so as to protect the welfare of these borrowers. We congratulate you on your industry and enterprise on speaking out on behalf of the people in the Windsor area.
As to the amount of interest being charged -and this matter is the subject of legislation which is now before this house-a study should be made to see what is an equitable rate. Having in mind the fact that few loans today are for $500 or less, and having in mind the large amount of work that is involved in the processing of a small loan, it may be that 2 per cent per month, which is the present rate, is not excessive. I am sure that the loan companies would have no objection to a considerably lower rate of interest on amounts in excess of $500. As a matter of fact I have discussed this matter with the head of a loan company. I have his letter which indicates that they would be quite pleased to have a lower rate of interest on amounts in excess of $500 up to, say, $1,500 or $2,000.
However, the people at large are not without fault. From a study of the report of the superintendent of insurance we find that those who apply for those loans are usually repeaters. They are persons who are continually in the hands of some loan company. They do not seem to be able to keep ahead with respect to their own financial dealings. They seem to need some paternal care. I think that is a further reason why we should see that the provisions of this act are extended. It seems to me that the average individual who takes out a loan from a moneylender is interested not so much in the amount of interest he is being charged or the other charges that are being added to his loan but rather is interested in how much a month he will be obliged to pay. The matter that interests him is, how much do I have to pay to get this loan? If he figures that he can pay that amount of money each month, he is quite satisfied.
If we are going to protect the general body of the public in Canada from the financial slavery of which we hear, I strongly recommend to the government that first of

The Address-Mr. Bell all the provisions of the Small Loans Act be extended to $2,000, so that in that act coverage will be given to an amount of $2,000; and further that there be an investigation-either departmental, by royal commission or otherwise, as the government may see fit-into the operation of all these personal loans up to an amount of $5,000.
