speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in congratulating the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and the seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and in welcoming the new members to this house, I should like to mention particularly the new hon. member from New Brunswick who is with us. To put the matter statistically, as the h'On. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) would, we have increased the Conservative representation from New Brunswick by one-third. If in the future we are able to get one-third as much for New Brunswick as we have been able to get in the past two years, we shall really be able to take our place in the economic sun.
During the by-election campaign it was my pleasure to spend a brief time in the constituency of Restigouche-Madawaska. While I should not like to hold myself out as an authority on all matters in that constituency,
I think there is a lesson to be learned by those senators, cabinet members and M.P.'s who came in from outside our province to take part in that campaign. I derived a great deal of personal satisfaction out of the result because I knew that the people up in the northern part of our province, by voting in the present hon. member, had completely rejected the election ideas those outsiders had when they came into New Brunswick. It certainly gave me a great deal of satisfaction to know that our French-speaking citizens and other people in New Brunswick were willing to make their own decision. As hospitable as we may be at other times, at election times we insist that certain conduct foreign to us be left at home.
Long before this session began, Mr. Speaker, it was obvious that economic conditions were looming large as points of discussion. It is in Canada the day of new heights of resource and capital investment. It is the day of prosperous economic conditions. It is in Canada the day of shattering gross national products. It is also the day of great national projects. I should like particular notice to be taken of that last reference, because it is my main theme in these few remarks.
Having said that we are in a period of great economic development in Canada, the question that immediately comes to mind is this. How are we in New Brunswick sharing 
in that development? I cannot do better than to quote from a review that was made by two professors at the University of New Brunswick. I refer to professors Smith and Whalen, both personal friends of mine. They are brilliant young men who undoubtedly could have proceeded west or elsewhere and done exceptionally well, as have a great many other maritimers. However, they have chosen to stay with us and help us during these crucial times. May I quote the first part of a review they did recently with respect to our economic development:
New Brunswick entered confederation in 1867 with a highly mature and prosperous economic system. The provincial economy was then based almost entirely on forest and sea, and these basic occupations sustained small agricultural, manufacturing, handicraft, and service industries. The techniques of wood, wind and water (that is, lumbering, shipbuilding and the carrying trade) were favourably developed during the first half of the nineteenth century in a province girt by the sea with a climate highly conducive to the growing of trees.
After 1880, however, the rate of economic growth in New Brunswick began to lag far behind that of the Canadian economy as a whole. This was due to a number of factors, including the development of the steamship, the construction of a national transcontinental rail system, the growth of protectionism, certain technological changes especially in manufacturing, and the opening of the Panama canal.
To put the matter in my own words, as applied to present-day circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I would say this. Personal income is perhaps the best indicator of our situation. To express it as a percentage of the Canadian personal per capita income, we know that our figure declined from 72-4 per cent in 1946 to 61-8 per cent in 1953. That is an alarming situation. In 1954, the latest year for which figures are available, we only reached the per capita personal income that the rest of Canada had attained in 1946.
It was natural, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that when the speech from the throne unfolded we should look for some definite word about a particular economic development that might help us in New Brunswick. We heard about pipe lines; we heard about wheat, but I am afraid there was no direct reference to anything that would materially assist us in this economic picture today. On January 12, at page 49 of Hansard the Prime Minister gave us some sort of an explanation for this omission from the speech from the throne. I quote his words:
I said we felt that parliament should not provide for sharing in the cost of provincial projects except in special circumstances and as a part of a policy which we could justify on national grounds.
Please notice those words, "national grounds", again, Mr. Speaker, because they

continue my theme. The situation in New Brunswick today is good so far as future possibilities are concerned. We have been fortunate in discovering new minerals in that province, and with the development of those we hope that the future will be much brighter. However, a snag has cropped up in our plans. We find that in order to locate smelters to refine the minerals in that province we must provide cheap electric power. We have potential power there, as everyone is aware, but we are not able to finance it properly. We do not have such resources in the provincial treasury, and it has been necessary to make appeals to the federal government for some sort of interest free or low interest loan. So far the federal government has not seen fit to assist us in this way. They have said it is a provincial matter and that they cannot possibly help us because it is not a national project. Please notice that reference again, Mr. Speaker; they said it was not a national project.
I ask very seriously here today, what is the difference between a pipe line out west which cannot possibly benefit us in the maritimes in any way, and one of our own local development projects such as the Beechwood project I have mentioned? On September 13, 1955, it was announced that a joint agreement between the federal government and the government of Ontario had been reached with respect to a plan of financing to assist the new Alberta pipe line. The principle is there, Mr. Speaker. There is direct assistance given by the federal and provincial governments. As I have said, we cannot see what difference there is between our own project and a project such as a pipe line.
Second, I would mention the seaway. We were very wary of the seaway. We were annoyed at the lack of consideration that was given to the future of maritime ports when the seaway was being talked about originally. We are growing more suspicious every day. During the past summer there were one or two items that came to light that bear out the fact our fears were not completely groundless. On November 10,	1955, Mr. Chevrier, in an address in Boston said this about the seaway:
A great increase in the flow of traffic between the St. Lawrence seaway area and the New England states was forecast here last night by Lionel Chevrier, president of the Canadian seaway authority.
He told members of the New England railroad club that this would result from expansion of industry and population in the seaway area which *'would be of advantage to both areas and the transportation lines that connect them."
The Address-Mr. Bell
''Rapid economic growth in both the United States and Canada is diminishing potential dislocating effects on existing transportation," Mr. Chevrier declared. "Industrial areas exchange traffic readily with other industrial areas and where the distances are not great the volume may become very large."
It was for this reason-with industrial expansion due to the seaway in mind-that he predicted a significant increase in what is now a relatively light flow of traffic between New England and central Canada.
Where do the maritimes fit into that prediction by Mr. Chevrier? Then we had a further cause for alarm with respect to the seaway when a strike occurred in Saint John. One of our large employers of labour, the sugar refinery was in a state of expansion, and as the result of a disagreement with the union it was found necessary to cease work. Negotiations were halted by both parties. Finally the matter was settled on December 8, and a significant statement was made by the management. It is worth noting that the management control of this organization is in central Canada. This is what they said:
Referring to union demands for a shorter work week, the statement said that throughout negotiations the company conceded that a 48-hour work week had become outmoded. It had "frankly and clearly put its cards on the negotiating table with respect to major location disadvantages which have been highlighted in an economic survey just completed, the major impact of which will be felt with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway."
This is the great national project that is going to help all of Canada. No, Mr. Speaker, we find it very difficult to see why it is that wheat can become a great national project; the South Saskatchewan dam can become a national project, yet one of our projects such as Beechwood, the development of a merchant navy or maritime coal, cannot be. The latter would seem to result in benefits to us all.
I suggest we have serious problems to overcome in the maritimes in our efforts to sell these ideas of ours. First we must sell the Canadian people the fact that we have a small diversified economy because of our location, our geography and the fact that we have no one particularly large industry. We will, therefore, always be in this category. We have no large rivers; we have nothing that fits into the Canadian economy which could possibly give us an opportunity of saying that it would benefit all the provinces. It must be appreciated from the beginning that we are small, and consideration must be given.
I feel that perhaps the more difficult problem that has to be overcome is what has been described as the Ottawa mentality. I refer to the politicians in Ottawa who refuse to look any farther than the Rideau canal.
384	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Bell They refuse to look down to the sea and realize that we do have an important part to play in the development of Canada. It has been said that we are a nation of landlubbers. That is true, Mr. Speaker. Instead of being a great maritime nation, we are controlled from central Canada. It really amuses me to hear people in this part of the country talk about these great national projects, and in the same breath refer to Sir John A. Macdonald's great national policies. He would have shuddered to think of some of the narrow-minded projects that seem to be considered national policies today.
We must revise our thinking with respect to these words that are bandied, about so much today, namely "national projects". With respect to these enterprises, everybody in Canada must take a look at them and think once again about what we mean when we say "national projects". The government is entirely to blame for hiding behind these words in the way they have been doing of late. Perhaps we are all to blame for not thinking correctly about them but I think we could go further and say that the government is taking unfair advantage of the use of those words.
A dominion-provincial conference was held last year. We arrived here with what we thought was a new approach to the matter. We had our own formula and proposals to make. In fact, I believe it was recognized on the floor of the conference that our proposals were most ingenious. We had a formula worked out which suggested that our per capita income should reach 85 per cent of the average per capita income of the dominion. We were not asking for 100 per cent, only 85 per cent. That meant that we were asking that the people in our part of the country should have a standard of living 85 per cent as good as the Canadian average. What happened? After some encouragement we now have some indication of what is to be given to the provinces?
In this connection I can only quote an editorial that appeared in the Globe and Mail of January 13 with respect to announcements that were made regarding the new tax agreement. I should also like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the Globe and Mail deserves a great deal of credit for the enlightened approach it is taking to the ills of the maritime provinces. It is very gratifying to all of us to see the tremendous interest the Globe and Mail is taking in the situation down there. All summer long there were very good articles on our conditions, and they are well aware of our problems.


In the final paragraph of the editorial the Globe and Mail sums up our arguments in much better language than I could use today. I quote:
Where fiscal need is fully apparent, as in the maritimes, the new formula is as inadequate as the old. If Ontario's contributions to British Columbia, Alberta and Quebec were lumped together and distributed to the maritime provinces, the national interest would be better served. And Ontario would be glad to make that contribution to the advancement of confederation's objectives.
Perhaps this is a new approach to this whole problem of ours. I have tried to point out the fears that are gripping our thinking with the ill-advised and ill-timed use of these words "national projects". I can only say in closing that it was a professor from the maritimes who is now out west, Professor Norman MacKenzie, who said that the provinces' economic welfare depends on Canada's prosperity. I ask, Mr. Speaker, how can Canada be prosperous when we have such a festering sore down east?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first of all like to join with the hon. members who have spoken in this debate in congratulating the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and the seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I would also like at the beginning to bring greetings from my home city of Edmonton, still the fastest growing city in Canada, we believe, and now popularly known as the home of the Grey cup.
On behalf of the people of Edmonton-Strathcona I would like to say how happy we were to have seen so many federal cabinet ministers out west during the past year. It is hoped that the members of the cabinet who did not get out west in 1955 will somehow or other find it possible to visit Alberta during the present year. Indeed, I hope that all eastern members of parliament, especially those who have not yet seen the west, will find some opportunity this year to pay us a visit. It seems likely that we may have another Grey cup match out west this year; and if we do, the city of Edmonton is looking forward to another very happy occasion at that time, and we think it would be appropriate for as many members of parliament from the east as possible to visit us on that occasion.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that all Alberta rejoiced when the Prime Minister found it possible to come out to Alberta early in September to participate in the celebration of our golden jubilee. His visit on that occasion was reminiscent of the visit of Sir Wilfrid Laurier at the time of the inauguration of the province of Alberta 50 years ago. On behalf of the people whom I have the honour to represent I should like

again to express my thanks to the Prime Minister for taking time off to visit us on that occasion, in spite of the very arduous responsibilities which he carries at all times here in Ottawa.
I should also like to compliment the government on the fact that the speech from the throne gives every indication that our country will continue to enjoy prosperity during the next 12 months. While there may be some soft spots in our economy, such as the wheat surplus that we have heard so much about in the last week, I am confident that the government will do whatever needs to be done to bring those soft spots into line with the general high level of our national prosperity. I should like to commend the government on the steps it has already proposed. They will be a big help to our farmers out west, who are hard pressed for ready cash. However, further steps may be necessary, and if they are I am sure our government will not be found lacking.
I have already placed a resolution on the order paper concerning the wheat surplus, and I shall refrain from making any further reference to it at the present time. However, there are some matters that I should like to draw to the attention of the government.
In recent months we have had considerable publicity in northern Alberta on the subject of our northern Alberta Indians. This publicity has quite rightly caused a good deal of concern amongst those who feel very keenly for this particular ethnic group who make up part of our population. Personally I am convinced that there is a good deal of hardship, if not actual distress, amongst our northern Alberta Indians. This opinion is based upon reports I have received from what I consider to be very reliable sources.
I would like to state here and now that I very definitely do not consider myself to be an authority on Indian affairs. I doubt, in fact, that we have very many authorities on Indian affairs in this parliament at the present time. However, the Indians are our problem, and we must do our best to deal with it as adequately as we can. I believe it is one of the most difficult problems we face in Canada today.
I am sure there is not one of us who would not like to see our Indian population taking their full and rightful place in our national, social and economic life, with full citizenship status. I believe that is the goal we have for our Indian population, or at least I hope it is.
But we must be realistic. I think we must face the fact that many Indians are not yet ready, and probably will not be ready for some time, to become fully integrated with the rest of our population. I think it can be 67509-25
The Address-Mr. Hanna said that our Indians are free to move about in our society if they so desire, but unfortunately most of them have chosen a sort of self-imposed isolation. The reason for this unfortunate situation appears to be a combination of lack of education, lack of trade skills, language and other cultural barriers.
I believe another motive behind this self-imposed isolation is their natural desire for self-preservation, the idea that if they forsake their reserves they are in danger of losing everything. I believe that somehow or other we have to persuade them that they should find a better way of life, and we should try to have them leave the reservations and find employment in the general population.
There are those who go so far as to say that some Indians are gradually losing ground as the other elements of our Canadian civilization advances steadily. I do not consider myself a judge of this situation, but if there is any truth in it, it is certainly deplorable. But of one thing we are certain, and that is that there need not be any real distress amongst our Indian population. If there is such distress, and it has been reported among northern Alberta Indians, then immediate and effective relief is most essential. Better rations and better clothing for those in need must certainly come before such long-term remedies as better education. But mere relief is not the answer to the problem, and relief must not be made more attractive than work.
Some Indian bands in Alberta and probably in other parts of Canada are well-off financially through oil leases and the like. However, it appears they are still not getting very much nearer to the goal of full and complete citizenship. Therein lies the core of the problem. I am afraid I must admit that I am an environmentalist in this respect. If we do not do something really effective to change the Indians' environment we will continue to have Canadian Indians rather than just plain Canadians.
We should, I believe, give more encouragement than we do to those who are ready to leave the reservations and make their livelihood amongst the general population. We must take measures to combat this self-imposed segregation which perpetuates the problem.
It may very well be asked, "What do you propose to do about it?" Briefly I propose that our short-range and long-term programs should be more effective, and they must be speeded up. Our progress in bringing up the Indian has been so slow that I am convinced we have not sufficient supervisors and other workers in the field.

The Address-Mr. Hanna
I would like at this time to pay unstinting tribute to those Indian agents, teachers, doctors, nurses and missionaries who have worked so hard, and are working so hard, at this most difficult problem. But I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the job is virtually overwhelming those workers who are in the field. I am convinced that our present rate of progress is so slow that in northern Alberta, at least, we are not getting anywhere.
I believe we must be prepared to vote more money to help solve our Indian problem. This is needed to place more workers in the field, and to speed up our education program. The immediate cause of hardship amongst the northern Indians appears to be the depletion of game, due to the advance of white settlement. This has deprived the Indians of their traditional livelihood and reduced them to a marginal existence dependent on relief.
I see it is approaching six o'clock, but perhaps I may be permitted to complete this subject.

We must as quickly as possible convince them that they ought to find alternative ways of making a living. Surely it is possible to demonstrate to them that they would enjoy a much better life in work other than hunting, fishing, and trapping. At the moment they appear not to have the necessary skills. We must therefore adopt the quickest way possible to train them in agriculture, lumbering, mining and construction work. There is no question about the need for farm labour and workers in the lumbering industry, but we have not so far persuaded very many Indians that these occupations would offer them a better way of life.
Nearly 150 years ago Thomas Jefferson said of the Indian problem:
Encourage them to abandon hunting, to apply themselves to the raising of stock, to agriculture, and to domestic manufacture, and thereby prove to themselves that less land and labour will maintain them: and bring within their reach more and more of the things which would help them make the transition.
In that connection I should like to make two comments. First, I agree with it; second, in a century and a half nobody seems to have done very much about it. Much has been said in the chamber in praise of the Colombo plan, and quite rightly so, but

what we need is a little Colombo plan for our Indian population. If it works in southeast Asia it should work at home. We have to speed up the program of helping them to help themselves, rather than merely giving them relief. Direct relief, surely, where it is needed; but it ought not to be needed in times like these.
Having said all this, I should like to compliment the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) upon the measures he has taken already to solve the Indian problem. There is no doubt that much good work is being done by many devoted workers. Under the present and former ministers the work of Indian education is being speeded up and many new schools have been opened. The other day I was reading in the Edmonton Journal about an excellent experiment which is being conducted in the town of Jasper Place on the outskirts of Edmonton. Here 60 Indian children are being brought in daily by school bus to attend the town schools with other Canadian children. Everyone connected with this plan deserves the highest praise, for I am sure this sort of thing will pay dividends. All these young Canadians will surely benefit by growing up together.
I should like also to compliment the minister upon the measures he has taken to have Indian children attend technical schools in Alberta. He has also made arrangements to co-operate with the Alberta department of agriculture so that agricultural short courses will be given on Alberta reservations. I hope that measures such as this will be rapidly expanded to embrace as many as possible of our Indian population.
The minister has indicated that he intends to go out west at the first opportunity and study the problems of our northern Indians at first hand. I hope he will find it possible to do this, as I would like him to see for himself what needs to be done.
On motion of Mr. Hanna the debate was adjourned.
